items.title: Matteo Thun designs Torre Velasca interiors using "building itself as the starting point"
items.text: Cajsa Carlson Editor 8 November 2026 Photography by Alberto Strada (unless stated otherwise) Italian architect Matteo Thun looked to the original materials and colours of Milan’ s iconic Torre Velasca when creating its new interiors, which feature pink hues inspired by the tower’s dusky facade. Thun has designed 72 flats in the upper floors of the tower, ranging from suites to duplex penthouses. He approached the interior design of the skyscraper, built in the 1950s by the architecture studio BBPR , with a focus on reinterpretation. Above and top photo by Ester Zanus Photographs Close “We allowed the masters and the building itself to speak, imagining a way of living within it that would carry the building a little further into the future, adding a new chapter to its history,” Thun told Dezeen. “We did not seek contrast: our design was informed directly by the materials and colours of Torre Velasca, and we chose not to intervene where we felt the architecture had already achieved a sense of completeness.” His studio preserved original details, including doors, window frames, loggias and tiles in the bathrooms and kitchens. These were then juxtaposed with modern furniture and evergreen design classics. “The interiors bring together new furniture designed by the studio and design references spanning the 1950s to the 1980s, including iconic pieces developed in new colourways in collaboration with historic Milanese companies,” Thun said. “With a deep appreciation for craftsmanship and a strong attention to detail, these designs share an ability to evolve without losing their identity.” The colour palette, too, was inspired by the original hues of the Torre Velasca. In the living rooms, walls are covered in custom-made velvet wall coverings by textile company Dedar in a pale pink colour that resembles the pink plaster on Torre Velasca’s facade. “The building itself was our starting point,” Thun said. “The pink plaster, developed and patented specifically for the tower, together with the blue and green floor tiles found both inside and in the loggias, formed the basis of our colour palette,” he continued. “We developed different gradations of these tones, opting for darker shades of green and blue to define the entrance areas and bedrooms. “ Photo by Ester Zanus As well as the apartments, Thun also designed the interior of the reception, lobby and the corridors on the ground floor. And while this was an interior project, Thun says it ended up becoming “a lesson in architecture” for his studio. “Working with a building as distinctive as Torre Velasca challenged us to think and work first and foremost as architects,” Thun said. “The challenge was not to reinvent the building, but to find ways to make its original character feel relevant today, while remaining true to BBPR’s vision,” he continued. “In this sense, the project became a process of discovery, with the building itself serving as our greatest teacher. It was, in many ways, a lesson in architecture for us.” Thun has previously designed the interior of the boutique hotel The Julius Prague and “hotel-like” rooms for a German hospital . Photography by Alberto Strada (unless stated otherwise) Read more Interiors

items.title: Linehouse reimagines industrial aesthetics for Jen Hangzhou hotel in Kohn Pedersen Fox-designed building
items.text: Christina Yao 5 November 2026 Photography by Jonathan Leijonhufvud and Wen Studio International studio Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou , China , which features details that nod to local craft and the area’s industrial heritage. The hotel, which is owned by the Shangri-La Hotel Group , is located along Hangzhou’s Dongxin River in an urban setting and flanked by two former industrial factory compounds. Plans and drawings Close The 18-floor hotel building was designed by US architecture firm Kohn Pedersen Fox , using steel, grey brick and glass to reference the site’s industrial past. The same design approach was extended into the interior by Linehouse , which focuses on showcasing local craft and nods to the industrial elements of the former factories. “Jen Hangzhou is an urban hotel that celebrates its neighbourhood context – one that layers history, craft, culture and rich materiality into a new perspective on Hangzhou,” Linehouse said. The studio used earth-toned marble, oak panelling and relaxed furniture in the ground-floor lobby to create a calm and warm atmosphere. At the entrance, guests are greeted by a textured artwork by artist Elsa Jeandedieu that depicts an abstract version of the bridges and canal close to the hotel. Patchwork patterns on the marble floor and on a bespoke rug in the lobby were informed by the street layout and tile patterns of the surrounding neighbourhood. Public areas Close All the hospitality spaces, including a restaurant , a bar and function rooms are located on the sixth floor. The long, linear OpenHouse restaurant is wrapped by full-height glazing that invites natural light inside. A timber design feature spans the ceiling and was informed by the craft of sunmao, a traditional timber joinery technique. It is highlighted by a thin black metal frame that supports suspended lighting. At the centre of the restaurant, a coffee bar splits the space into a dining area on one side and an all-day lounge on the other. In the private dining room, the timber canopy has an angled design and is decorated with burnt red and yellow hues. In the rest of the OpenHouse restaurant, rooms feature teal tiles and handmade ceramic wall lighting. The adjacent Koan Bar is a triple-height venue characterised by an undulating black metal staircase that takes guests to a terrace on the upper floor, with incorporated platforms where guests can socialise. The sinuous staircase is carved between walls lined with concrete panels, another nod to the site’s industrial heritage. Beneath it, curved booths in walnut timber and tan leather provide intimate seating spaces. Three interconnected spaces on the sixth floor, enveloped by undulating timber walls, will be used for events and intimate social gatherings. Like in the lobby, bespoke carpets feature patterns abstracted from urban details in the neighbourhood. The seventh floor is dedicated to wellness and comprises a gym, a yoga room, a spa, a pool and changing rooms, made from tactile materials with muted tones to create a calm environment. At the gym, a lava stone wall has engravings that illustrate movement, while the yoga room features hand-chiseled timber panels. A sloped skylit annex accommodates the swimming pool . The 176 guest rooms were conceived as “urban retreats”. Here, Linehouse used a restrained palette of gun metal, oak datum, textured render and tan leather to underline the industrial aesthetic. Guest rooms Close “The public areas explore traditional craft techniques such as sunmao timber joinery, clay tiling and bricks, natural patterns, textures and renders, whilst the guestrooms explore a refined industrial aesthetic,” Linehouse said. “Red brick, concrete, metal and bold forms reference the surrounding industrial environment whilst handcrafted tiles, vintage timber, colours and metals with different patinas introduce warmth, richness and texture.” The guest rooms have curved ceilings that create indirect lighting and add softness to the space, while the bathrooms are illuminated by glass-block walls. Founded by Alex Mok and Briar Hickling in 2013, Linehouse is an architecture and interior practice with studios in Shanghai, Hong Kong and Auckland. It has recently designed Ink Ink Market in Shanghai with a translucent sloping facade , as well as the interiors for Bangkok’s Central Park shopping centre with three dramatic atriums , which was shortlisted of Retail Interior (large) by this year’s Dezeen Awards . Project credits Area: 12,850 sqm Client: Kerry Properties Operator: Shangri-La Design principal: Alex Mok Design team: Wang Jue, Jingru Tong, Yunbin Lou, Cherngyu Chen, Inez Low, Yeling Guo, Aiwen Shao, Mia Zhou, Norman Wang, Yuechen Wu Lighting: LPA Decorative lighting: Kris Lite, Van Collection, Yi Design, Yun Zhao Studio, Fine Lumens, Santa & Cole, Audo, Timothy Oulton, La Nuit Design consultant: EDGE Design Interior contractor: Terart Decoration Design & Engineering Co., Ltd, Shenzhen Lead management consultant: Wong & Ouyang (HK) Ltd. LDI & structural consultant: Zhejiang Province Institute of Architectural Design and Research MEP engineer consultant: Hangzhou MJP Mechanical & Electrical Design Consultant Ltd. Photography by Jonathan Leijonhufvud and Wen Studio Read more Interiors Exclusives

items.title: "Direct and unrefined" materials create tactile interior at Jeju restaurant by &Daughters
items.text: Cajsa Carlson Editor 4 November 2026 Canadian studio &Daughters used basalt, cork , concrete, thatch and wood to design Jeju, a Korean restaurant in Vancouver that features traditional touches in a contemporary interior. The architect’s starting point for the design was the restaurant’s menu, which includes modern dishes developed by chef Dylan Kim, traditional dishes created by his mother, chef Myungseok “Julie” Suh and dishes that they created together. Jeju’s interior is a mix of different tactile materials “The restaurant exists in the space where these two narratives meet,” &Daughters principal Emma Sims told Dezeen. “We began to think of tradition and reinterpretation as the foundation for the design, translating this relationship into a physical space through a specific set of people, places, materials and traditions.” While Jeju’s exterior has a modern steel-mesh facade, the interior juxtaposes wood and concrete for a warmer, more tactile feel. A version of a traditional thatched house is at the heart of the restaurant At the heart of the 44-seat restaurant is a reinterpretation of a traditional thatched house from Jeju Island, South Korea, called a chogajip. This was constructed using lumber and hand-thatched grass, and creates an artisanal focal point for the space. Other materials, including basalt, were chosen by &Daughters for Jeju to ensure a natural feel. Basalt was used for the bar, chef’s table and host stand, while cork cladding helps create a soft feel while adding acoustic dampening. &Daughters kept and polished an existing concrete floor The studio kept the existing concrete floor but polished it to reveal variations in its colour. “The palette is quite simple – basalt, cork, raw concrete masonry units, polished concrete, wood and thatch,” Sims said. “Basalt is one of the most recognisable materials of Jeju Island,” she continued. “Formed through volcanic activity, it is found throughout the island’s landscape, architecture and traditional stone walls. Beyond that, we were interested in materials that felt direct and unrefined, allowing them to retain their natural character.” A traditional three-pole gate evokes Jeju Island Wood and cork create a warm atmosphere The studio wanted to “introduce elements of tradition, ritual and memory into the interior,” Sims said. As well as the thatched house, another traditional architectural feature from Jeju, a jeongnang three-pole gate, was also introduced to the interior. “Historically used as a means of communicating whether a household was home, away or nearby, it offered an alternative to a conventional locked entrance, rooted in trust and shared understanding,” Sims said. “At Jeju, we incorporated our interpretation into the glazing beside the entrance, where staff lower two poles each day to signal that the restaurant is open and guests are welcome, raising them again at the end of service,” she continued. “In this way, a traditional architectural element becomes an active part of the restaurant’s daily life.” Other restaurants recently featured on Dezeen include a brick-clad eatery in London’s Soho area and a bistro in Montreal influenced by Japanese metabolism . items.title: Em-Estudio lines Mexico City bar with walls of books
items.text: Dan Howarth 31 October 2026 Photography by Nin Solis (unless stated otherwise) The vintage bookstores of Mexico City ‘s Roma neighbourhood influenced the interiors of this basement bar , designed by local outfit Em-Estudio. Located below an early 20th-century house in the Mexican capital’s historic colonia, Libreria Valladolid was designed to evoke the experience of exploring old bookshops. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Photography Close “It captures the thrill felt when entering these places, searching for a unique story that has patiently waited among thousands of books on all topics and from many eras,” said Em-Estudio . Accessed from the street through an unassuming door, the entry vestibule features shelves packed with old volumes and more stacks along a wooden staircase that descends to another threshold. Photo by Rene Villaseñor Small lamps are squeezed between the spines and placed on top of the stacks, creating a moody glow that sets the scene for the bar beyond. “The old bookstore is encountered upon entering, as you descend the stairs, and it remains behind as you cross the first threshold, where the books transform into the skin that embraces the rooms,” said the studio. Inside the basement, dark herringbone flooring and surfaces drenched in burgundy continue the bookshop atmosphere. The larger walls are lined entirely with shelves filled with books stacked spine inwards, so the warm beige of their pages faces the room. Cove lighting illuminates the books, creating a dramatic contrast with the otherwise shadowy bar, while banquettes below are accompanied by circular marble tables for placing drinks. “The pages of thousands of books resting on bookshelves that reach the ceiling shed their literal meaning, becoming a tapestry in shades of white that only time can give, bathed in a gradient of warm light,” Em-Estudio said. Other areas such as the DJ booth, the bar and the bathrooms are highlighted with gold leaf and brass to draw the eye. A further hidden lounge space is disguised by another bookshelf, decorated with cans and objects that “evoke a grocery-store bar”. This room swaps burgundy for green, applied in gloss across the ceiling and appearing in a long marble table that runs through the centre. Dark wood Van Beuren chairs with yellow upholstery are lined up along each side, parallel to more walls of books that are uplit along each shelf. A mirror that covers the back wall visually doubles the space, extending the table and the bookshelves in the reflection. Em-Estudio was co-founded by architect Ivan Esqueda and interior designer Gala Sánchez-Renero – a husband and wife who also operate individual practices. Their previous collaborations include a holiday home on a steep hillside in Oaxaca, Mexico, built from coloured concrete chosen to blend into the rocky mountainside. Project credits: Architecture and interior design: Taller Ivan Esqueda and Gala Sánchez-Renero Estudio Design team: Berenice Galindo, Sergio Peláez, Fabián Cedillo Construction and installations: Miguel Ángel Márquez Carpentry: Leonardo Cabrera Photography by Nin Solis (unless stated otherwise) Read more Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Atelier Zébulon Perron draws on metabolist influence for Montreal bistro
items.text: Ben Dreith US editor 30 October 2026 Photography by Alex Lesage A monochrome palette and influences from Japanese metabolism characterise Bistrot à Franky in Montreal , Canada designed by local outfit Atelier Zébulon Perron . The restaurant is a home base for local chef Francis Blais in the city’s hip Mile End neighbourhood. Photographs Close Atelier Zébulon Perron took what it views as the standard design language of a Montreal bistro – bright lighting and lots of activity – and translated it into a more contemporary design. For studio founder Zebulon Perron, the monochrome whites and beiges, interspersed with milled aluminium accents and a large zinc bar top, allowed the studio to experiment with textures and lighting to create visual interest and contrast in the dining space. “With the monochromy of the restaurant, we experimented with textures – shiny versus matte, tile nd and stucco – and how light reacts to those surfaces in different ways,” Perron told Dezeen. The studio emphasised the postmodern and “retrofuturist” elements of the design, pointing to the custom chandeliers with their illuminated Pyrex tubes and exposed wiring, fabricated by Perron’s long-time collaborators, local lighting design studio Lambert & Fils . Perron highlighted the milled aluminium wine cellar that sits above the bar face, interspersed with portholes that are a direct reference to Japanese metabolist architecture. “There’s a postmodern, 1980s aesthetic that naturally rose from everything we were doing,” said Perron. Visitors enter the restaurant through a red-painted hallway and a metal door and handle carved from butcher block by local cabinetmaker Olivier Doray . Inside, only the terrazzo floor was a holdover from the building’s former use. Granite tabletops cover some of the larger tables, while the classic bistrot white tablecloths are draped over the smaller tables. Blond leather banquettes were placed below large mirrors on the wall opposite the bar, and these larger seating arrangements are centred by large butcher block tables, also fabricated by Doray. Custom walnut chairs were designed by local industrial designer Guillaume Sasseville . On the walls, white tile is interspersed with stucco and works of art, curated by local filmmaker Xavier Dolan . These artworks give pops of colour and Perron said that the monochromatic design elements allow both the food and the artworks to stand out in the space. “Since the canvas is pretty neutral, the food and the artwork take centre stage,” he said. A set of windows opens up the kitchen space to the dining room. Custom bar seating features white columns with seats informed by transportation design, and Perron noted that the metal details and clean lines of the bar space, as well as the metal fans, also give the interior a streamlined look. Atelier Zébulon Perron has designed some of the most interesting interior spaces in the city, including Café Constance and the dining areas for the city’s Four Seasons hotel . It also helped create the pop-up bar staged during the city’s inaugural design week earlier this year. Photography by Alex Lesage Read more Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw
items.text: Amy Frearson Editor-at-large 30 October 2026 Photography by Sophia van den Hoek Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam , featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis . Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music. Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud . Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam. “We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen. The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach. Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek , a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport. Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline. “We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet. “We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.” The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis , who is Cournet’s partner. Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar. Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl. Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency . Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tylko’s shelving, which launched earlier this year. These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar. “There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet. “When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.” ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam. The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering. It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests. Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme. “Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet. “It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.” Photography by Sophia van den Hoek Read more Interiors

items.title: Simone is a Copenhagen bookstore that doubles as a gallery, event space or listening room
items.text: Amy Frearson Editor-at-large 29 October 2026 Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson Custom-designed furniture by Derya Arpac, Lærke Ryom, Kasper Kyster and Daniel Schofield sets the scene for this unconventional bookstore in the Danish capital. Simone Book Services is a Copenhagen shop specialising in rare and independent books and magazines, but it can also be an exhibition gallery, a listening space, or a venue for book launches and other informal gatherings. Turkish-born architect Arpac oversaw the intentionally “un-Scandinavian” interior, which includes modular shelves made from aluminium and cherry wood, mobile book trolleys and a counter dressed in leather. Gallery Close The concept for the store was born out of conversations between Arpac, who works for furniture brand &Tradition , and founders Tugce Kayar Subay and Ibo Subay, a married couple with backgrounds in fashion media and marketing. The Subays had amassed such an impressive collection of art, design and fashion literature that they launched a “literary branding” business in February 2026, curating libraries for exhibitions, offices and brand spaces. Simone gives the couple a physical platform for this business and allows it to evolve further. It showcases their curation of books and magazines, but also furniture and objects related to reading culture. “Tugce is the book nerd, and I’m the design nerd; we came up with this idea of combining our passions,” Arpac told Dezeen. “We wanted to create a space where people would come and be inspired.” Arpac’s own contribution to the space is a system of wall-mounted shelves crafted from cherry, a red-hued hardwood that offers a different aesthetic to traditional Scandinavian timbers like oak, ash or pine. “The shelving appears to extend and climb through the space, almost like scaffolding or the structural skeleton of a building,” she said. The leather-wrapped counter was designed by Ryom , who specialises in alternative methods of upholstery. Similar to the Garments chairs she developed for The Mindcraft Project , the bar’s edges feature zippers that open up to reveal storage areas. Kyster developed a shelving system made from folded sheets of unpolished aluminium, intended for displaying magazines. The system is modular, so more panels could be added in future. For seating, Schofield crafted a bench out of sheets of black-pigmented MDF that slots neatly into the store’s corner. It’s joined by mobile book trolleys made from the same material, encouraging visitors to move books around the space. In addition to the four designers, artist Staffan Sundström was invited to create paintings for the bookstore. He contributed three pieces for the store opening, although the display will change as works are sold. The store also includes an area dubbed “the red room”, a David Lynch-inspired space featuring red walls and matching floor-to-ceiling curtains. This 20-square-metre space offers scope for small-scale events and exhibitions. Since opening, Simone has hosted various events, including a book launch for photographer Lasse Dearman, a curated library for sports brand ASICS and a pop-up for fashion label Bonnetje Recut. Future ambitions include the launch of “reading objects”, including everything from bookmarks and paperweights to lighting and shelving. Photography by Armin Tehran and Hampus Berndtson Read more Interiors

items.title: OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca
items.text: Amy Frearson Editor-at-large 27 October 2026 Photography by Jose Hevia Mallorca-based architecture and interiors studio OHLAB has overseen the design of a hotel in Palma, including a renovated heritage building from 1935 and a new structure built from cross-laminated timber and cork . The 41-room Terreno Barrio Hotel was envisioned as “a catalyst for the neighbourhood” of El Terreno, in the west of the Mallorcan city, serving as a community hub as well as a destination for tourists. Drawings and photographs Close Ground floor plan Section Section concept diagram Floor plan concept diagram “Terreno is not conceived as a tourist object imposed on its context, but as a device for exchange – a hotel that, before being a hotel, aims to be an extension of the barrio,” said OHLAB founders Paloma Hernaiz and Jaime Oliver. “This is not a slogan; it is the principle that orders programme, thresholds, atmospheres and materiality.” The new building stands alongside a renovated heritage block from 1935 The hotel’s reception is in the renovated 1935 building, a five-storey apartment block designed by local architect Francesc Casas, along with the restaurant and bar, a club, and a roof bar. OHLAB refers to this building as “the stage”, the eye-catching focal point of the complex, while the new structure is described as “the bazaar”, its civic heart. Wrapping a new public plaza, this second block houses the community-led spaces, including a cafe, coworking areas, a bookshop and gallery, pop-up retail, a gym, a spa and a cinema. A ramped floor features the same red as the hotel logo OHLAB adopted different strategies for the architecture and interior design of the two structures, creatively exploring the themes of building and material reuse in various ways. “Here, circularity was understood not only as an environmental or material strategy, but also as an economic, social and territorial one, a way of keeping value within the local ecosystem by activating residents, culture, crafts, suppliers and everyday life,” they said. In the renovated building, interior design revives the existing structure rather than covering it. Communal spaces have a theatrical character, with patterned floor tiles and heavy curtains. Highlights include a golden mirror bar and a wool curtain installation by artist Sylvia Sanchez Montoya . A wool curtain installation by Sylvia Sanchez Montoya features in the reception and restaurant OHLAB’s red bar stools front a polished brass bar In the bedrooms, colourblocking creates a horizontal divide between top and bottom. Floors and furniture feature matching terrazzo, produced by local tile manufacturer Huguet using the project’s demolition waste. In the bedrooms, colourblocking divides the rooms into two halves Materials are even more prominent in the seven-storey new building, thanks to the choice of materials. Cork clads the courtyard-facing north facade, while the other exterior walls feature timber louvres that shade the windows from direct sunlight. Inside, the exposed CLT structure is brought to life through more playful use of colour and materials. The cafe and shop is a key example, with shades of brown and lime green extending across to the terrazzo floors and wooden furniture. Bedrooms in the new building feature murals by artist Albert Pinya The bedrooms in this block have a different character, with murals by Mallorcan artist Albert Pinya , bathrooms housed inside mirrored boxes, and timber flooring that merges with joinery. OHLAB was appointed by José Taltavull, who developed the concept for the hotel after being brought on board by hotelier Lydia Piñero. Taltavull appointed graphic design office StudioRoses to oversee the hotel’s visual identity, which fed into OHLAB’s scheme. Various elements were picked out in the same red as the hotel logo, including the ramped floor between the bar and reception, the stage in the club, and the sculptural stools located in the bar. Most of the furniture was either designed by OHLAB or sourced from Mallorca-based manufacturers. A DJ table was made from cork leftover from the construction, while Mallorcan artist Pedro Óliver contributed the neon lighting pieces that feature throughout. StudioRoses designed the hotel’s visual identity, including the logo and signage The new building features flexible co-working, cafe and retail spaces Terreno Barrio Hotel is the latest in a series of major openings in Palma in recent years, with the city in the midst of a cultural renaissance. El Terreno is a major part of that story, particularly since Mallorca-based shoe brand Camper completed its 15,000-square-metre Project Gomila in 2023, which includes the new Jasper Morrison-designed Can Pa bakery . OHLAB’s other projects in the city include the Can Santacilia residential development and the Paral·lel apartment complex . Project credits : Client: Grupo Piñero Concept: José Taltavull Branding and initial brief: José Taltavull, Studio Roses, Joan Alvares Graphic design: Studio Roses Architecture and interior design: OHLAB OHLAB team: Paloma Hernaiz and Jaime Oliver with Robin Harloff, Juan Carlos Martínez, Carlos Garijo, Lara Ortega, Maria Bruna Pisciotta, Sonia Hernan, María Dominguez, Bárbara Beltrán, Elisa Lazzarotto, Pablo Sinan, Loreto Angulo, Marta Carvalho, Wiktoria Krapiec, Camila Ospina, Laura Barros, Sofía Galdame, Maja Stankowska, Mateusz Baranowski, Natalie Battah, Thea Schütz, Zheng Xiagyuan, Izabella Warcaba, Eirini Papadatou, Katerina Rangelova Quantity surveyor: Jorge Ramón Project management: Jorge Ramón, Rafa del Toro Structural engineering: HIMA HVAC/MEP engineering: INGENIO CLT timber structure: Egoin Passive House consultant: Plus Aurea LEED consultant: PGI Acoustic consultant: Tafor, Ambient Acoustics Sound consultant: INTRVL, Ibasa Lighting consultant (club and wool curtain): INTRVL Landscape design: Verdsatile Landscape execution: Amor Photography by Jose Hevia Read more Architecture Interiors

items.title: Box 9 used “brick on every surface” in Soho restaurant Kid
items.text: Cajsa Carlson Editor 20 October 2026 Photography by Andrew Urwin Local studio Box 9 has used bricks made from recycled construction waste for the interior of London restaurant Kid, where the material clads everything from the grill to the wine room. Photographs Close The 307-square-metre restaurant in central Soho sits on a corner and is made from two formerly separate units, which Box 9 combined to make Kid , a modern take on a Turkish mangal restaurant. While the Frith Street side of the restaurant has a more traditional Victorian feel, the Bateman Street side was given a contemporary design, with the use of brick joining the two sites. “The site’s two shopfronts offered an opportunity to connect their contrasting elevations through a shared design approach,” Box 9 co-founder Lou Davies told Dezeen. “Frith Street retains a beautiful Victorian upper storey with distinctive brick patterns that reflect Soho’s merchant-trading history, while Bateman Street has a new elevation and a central section rising to the residences above,” she continued. “The building itself suggested uniting the spaces with a single material.” Brick was chosen not just because of its use in the building the restaurant is located in, but also because of its connection to traditional hospitality spaces and the Turkish heritage of Kid chef Sertaç Dirik. “Brick became central to the concept because it connected so many elements of the project,” Davies explained. “It has a centuries-old relationship with restaurants, kitchens and cooking with fire, forming the basis of traditional fireplaces and hearths,” she continued. “It also reflected the heritage of Turkish cooking and Sertaç’s family background, while connecting to the history of the Soho building and its original brick patterns.” Guests enter the two-storey Kid restaurant through a discreet door on Bateman Street, where they are met by a large, central grill. Like most of the interior at Kid, this was made from material company Kenoteq ’s K-Briq, which is crafted from at least 90 per cent recycled construction and demolition waste and requires no fossil fuels or firing to produce. According to Box 9, this means that it releases a tenth of the carbon emissions of traditional fired-clay bricks. “We loved the idea of using brick on every surface,” Davies said of the material choice. “There was a raw humbleness to it: wine cellars, kitchens and grills would traditionally have been built with brick,” she continued. “It wasn’t about fancy materials; it was about using the best material for the purpose.” Upstairs, visitors will also find the wine room, which seats 14 people and was similarly made entirely of brick. The studio chose slightly different designs to define the two upstairs rooms, using a traditional bond with a traditional joint for the Victorian side and a soldier bond and a raked joint for the more contemporary section. Downstairs, Box 9 designed Kid’s open bakery, which features moveable bespoke tables by design firm Jan Hendzel Studio to allow the room to be used as an events space. Overall, the main aim for Box 9 was to create a space that would complement Dirik’s food, which was formed through his cooking at his family’s restaurant Mangal II. “We needed to create a completely unique restaurant that represented Serta,” Davies concluded. “His personality is big, and his background is rooted in generations of cooking in Turkey and his family’s cooking style, as well as how they cooked at Mangal II. All his training was in cooking with fire.” London has seen a spate of recent restaurant openings, including a French-style restaurant by Cassette and a London pizzeria designed by Isern Serra . Photography by Andrew Urwin Read more Interiors
designers: Cassette and a London pizzeria designed by Isern Serra

items.title: NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"
items.text: Jane Englefield Design and interiors reporter 19 October 2026 Photography by Piercarlo Quecchia (unless stated otherwise) Local studio NM3 looked to Vienna’s iconic 20th-century American Bar by Adolf Loos when designing the bespoke red-hued interior of Milan’s Bar Bardo. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos’s famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Photography Close “The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference,” studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. “The ambition was never to recreate Loos’s bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann’s Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project,” he explained. “Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character.” Located just across the road from the city’s popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains for longer black ones. Photo by T-Space The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records. Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes. “By simply removing the furniture, the cocktail bar can easily be transformed into a club,” said Zorzi. “The flexibility of the space is therefore achieved through a simple architectural arrangement rather than complex spatial interventions.” At the back of the space, the striking bathroom was covered with bright red 10-centimetre-by-10-centimetre tiles, from floor to ceiling. Photo by T-Space Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected for the toilets, sink and other fixtures, while pared-back sconce lights illuminate the cubicles. Bar Bardo marks a softer design direction for NM3. The studio previously conceived a “raw” interior for Milan’s Galleria Montegani , as well as a similarly metal-heavy store in the city for fashion brand Miss Sixty. Ahead of Milan design week in April, NM3 was among the studios that spoke to Dezeen about what it’s like to be a contemporary designer in Italy’s design capital. Photography by Piercarlo Quecchia (unless stated otherwise) Read more Interiors Exclusives
designers: T-Space Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected

items.title: Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue and gold Bangkok cafe interior
items.text: Cajsa Carlson Editor 19 October 2026 Photography by Pichan Sujaritsatit Japanese studio I IN drew on traditional Thai festivals, where thousands of paper lanterns are released into the sky, when creating the interior for the first Blue Bottle Coffee cafe in Bangkok . The interior of the cafe is dominated by the large Blue Lantern installation above the coffee counter. Gallery Close “The main idea came from Thailand’s traditional lantern festival,” I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen. “We wanted to capture the feeling of a lantern floating in the sky and bring that into the space in a contemporary way.” “This became what we call the Blue Lantern, a large sculptural element extending from the ceiling above the drip station,” he continued. As it is the brand’s first cafe in Bangkok, the studio wanted to design a “bold and dramatic” space that would also nod to local culture. “The lantern idea came from the local culture, and from the beginning, we wanted to make it as large and impactful as possible,” Terui said. “We placed it at the location where customers first enter the cafe, so it would immediately catch their attention and become a symbol of the store.” The furniture and fixtures in the 178-square-metre cafe were made from teak wood, a material that is often avoided in the West due to concerns about illegal logging , but which is local to Thailand. “Every country has their own approach to natural materials, depending on what is locally available and traditionally used,” Terui said. “In Thailand, especially in the north, teak is a very familiar material and commonly used in the interiors and architecture.” Blue Bottle Coffee cafe Bangkok is drenched in blue hues, with the brand’s signature colour used for the lantern and coffee counter. For the rest of the space, I IN chose a pale blue colour to “give guests a sense of brand identity and the feeling of a sky,” Terui explained. After visiting the city, the designer also decided to add gold details to the cafe interior. “The idea of bringing gold into the interior actually came from my personal experience of walking around Bangkok,” Terui said. “As you walk through the city, you suddenly come across these beautiful, strong gold colours, and I found this contrast very unique,” he continued. “It was something that stayed in my memory of Bangkok, and I wanted to bring a little of that feeling into the cafe.” I IN also recently designed the concrete Andersson Bell store in Tokyo and clad the Human Made store in Seoul in handcrafted tiles . Photography by Pichan Sujaritsatit Read more Interiors
designers: the large Blue Lantern installation above the coffee counter

items.title: Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for London restaurant Cassette
items.text: Rachael Gilby 12 October 2026 Design studio Gundry & Ducker has renovated the interiors of a Grade II-listed workshop for Cassette, a Parisian-style bistro that has recently opened in the heart of London ‘s West End. The spacious eatery is housed within a nineteenth-century gothic building, which features double-height ceilings and an expansive glass facade with intricate detailing. The design was informed by traditional Parisian bistros Located in Covent Garden, the restaurant spans 107 square metres and accommodates 52 customers across a ground floor dining room and a basement level. An outdoor terrace welcomes an additional 30 guests when the weather permits. “Our brief talked about a neighbourhood restaurant in the centre of town,” Gundry & Ducker co-founder Tyeth Gundry told Dezeen. “From there, the conversation centred on familiarity, recognition and ease – creating a neighbourhood restaurant for friends who live in different parts of the city.” The studio chose a warm, neutral colour palette for the interior The studio intended for the design to resemble traditional Parisian establishments by incorporating familiar elements, including deep aubergine finishes, dark banquette seating and classic bentwood bistro chairs. Alongside this, the designers combined natural fabrics, sapele wood and stainless steel with exposed brickwork to create a restrained colour palette and an overall “deliberately unfussy” interior. The design combines a mixture of dark woods with natural fabrics and stainless steel “We talked a lot about colour: summer park landscapes, Parisian bistros and wine,” Gundry explained. “Tone too was really important; we needed colours that would dim well to help us create a low-level evening setting that feels warm; the key to which is controlling reflected light,” he continued. The Grade II-listed interior has double-height ceilings and a large glass facade Taking cues from the surrounding theatre district, the studio installed a sophisticated sound system and a statement curtain with acoustic qualities that wraps around the main dining area. “We felt that we could explore the world of theatres given the restaurant’s location in London’s West End,” Gundry said. “By placing the curtain within gantry structures, they became theatre curtains and added some character to the space,” he continued. “In this case, acoustics was as much part of the conversation as colour or operation. The curtains help to control reverb and talk about a softer acoustic.” A statement curtain wraps around the top of the main dining room Cassette’s owners, Mark Gurney and Matt Bushnell, sourced a selection of artworks from local markets and car boot sales to add pops of colour and personality into the space. Other restaurant interiors recently featured on Dezeen include Bétyle Studio’s design for Parisian eatery Arcane 17 and the newly opened Skywalker Grill located in the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Los Angeles . Read more Interiors
designers: placing the curtain within gantry structures

items.title: Linehouse reimagines industrial aesthetics for Jen Hangzhou hotel in Kohn Pedersen Fox-designed building
items.summary:
International studio Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou, China, which features details that nod to local craft and the area's industrial heritage. 
 The post  Linehouse reimagines industrial aesthetics for Jen Hangzhou hotel in Kohn Pedersen Fox-designed building  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Christina Yao 5 November 2026 Photography by Jonathan Leijonhufvud and Wen Studio International studio Linehouse has completed the interiors of the Jen hotel in Hangzhou , China , which features details that nod to local craft and the area’s industrial heritage. The hotel, which is owned by the Shangri-La Hotel Group , is located along Hangzhou’s Dongxin River in an urban setting and flanked by two former industrial factory compounds. Plans and drawings Close The 18-floor hotel building was designed by US architecture firm Kohn Pedersen Fox , using steel, grey brick and glass to reference the site’s industrial past. The same design approach was extended into the interior by Linehouse , which focuses on showcasing local craft and nods to the industrial elements of the former factories. “Jen Hangzhou is an urban hotel that celebrates its neighbourhood context – one that layers history, craft, culture and rich materiality into a new perspective on Hangzhou,” Linehouse said. The studio used earth-toned marble, oak panelling and relaxed furniture in the ground-floor lobby to create a calm and warm atmosphere. At the entrance, guests are greeted by a textured artwork by artist Elsa Jeandedieu that depicts an abstract version of the bridges and canal close to the hotel. Patchwork patterns on the marble floor and on a bespoke rug in the lobby were informed by the street layout and tile patterns of the surrounding neighbourhood. Public areas Close All the hospitality spaces, including a restaurant , a bar and function rooms are located on the sixth floor. The long, linear OpenHouse restaurant is wrapped by full-height glazing that invites natural light inside. A timber design feature spans the ceiling and was informed by the craft of sunmao, a traditional timber joinery technique. It is highlighted by a thin black metal frame that supports suspended lighting. At the centre of the restaurant, a coffee bar splits the space into a dining area on one side and an all-day lounge on the other. In the private dining room, the timber canopy has an angled design and is decorated with burnt red and yellow hues. In the rest of the OpenHouse restaurant, rooms feature teal tiles and handmade ceramic wall lighting. The adjacent Koan Bar is a triple-height venue characterised by an undulating black metal staircase that takes guests to a terrace on the upper floor, with incorporated platforms where guests can socialise. The sinuous staircase is carved between walls lined with concrete panels, another nod to the site’s industrial heritage. Beneath it, curved booths in walnut timber and tan leather provide intimate seating spaces. Three interconnected spaces on the sixth floor, enveloped by undulating timber walls, will be used for events and intimate social gatherings. Like in the lobby, bespoke carpets feature patterns abstracted from urban details in the neighbourhood. The seventh floor is dedicated to wellness and comprises a gym, a yoga room, a spa, a pool and changing rooms, made from tactile materials with muted tones to create a calm environment. At the gym, a lava stone wall has engravings that illustrate movement, while the yoga room features hand-chiseled timber panels. A sloped skylit annex accommodates the swimming pool . The 176 guest rooms were conceived as “urban retreats”. Here, Linehouse used a restrained palette of gun metal, oak datum, textured render and tan leather to underline the industrial aesthetic. Guest rooms Close “The public areas explore traditional craft techniques such as sunmao timber joinery, clay tiling and bricks, natural patterns, textures and renders, whilst the guestrooms explore a refined industrial aesthetic,” Linehouse said. “Red brick, concrete, metal and bold forms reference the surrounding industrial environment whilst handcrafted tiles, vintage timber, colours and metals with different patinas introduce warmth, richness and texture.” The guest rooms have curved ceilings that create indirect lighting and add softness to the space, while the bathrooms are illuminated by glass-block walls. Founded by Alex Mok and Briar Hickling in 2013, Linehouse is an architecture and interior practice with studios in Shanghai, Hong Kong and Auckland. It has recently designed Ink Ink Market in Shanghai with a translucent sloping facade , as well as the interiors for Bangkok’s Central Park shopping centre with three dramatic atriums , which was shortlisted of Retail Interior (large) by this year’s Dezeen Awards . Project credits Area: 12,850 sqm Client: Kerry Properties Operator: Shangri-La Design principal: Alex Mok Design team: Wang Jue, Jingru Tong, Yunbin Lou, Cherngyu Chen, Inez Low, Yeling Guo, Aiwen Shao, Mia Zhou, Norman Wang, Yuechen Wu Lighting: LPA Decorative lighting: Kris Lite, Van Collection, Yi Design, Yun Zhao Studio, Fine Lumens, Santa & Cole, Audo, Timothy Oulton, La Nuit Design consultant: EDGE Design Interior contractor: Terart Decoration Design & Engineering Co., Ltd, Shenzhen Lead management consultant: Wong & Ouyang (HK) Ltd. LDI & structural consultant: Zhejiang Province Institute of Architectural Design and Research MEP engineer consultant: Hangzhou MJP Mechanical & Electrical Design Consultant Ltd. Photography by Jonathan Leijonhufvud and Wen Studio Read more Interiors Exclusives

items.title: OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca
items.summary:
Mallorca-based architecture and interiors studio OHLAB has overseen the design of a hotel in Palma, including a renovated heritage building from 1935 and a new structure built from cross-laminated timber and cork. The 41-room Terreno Barrio Hotel was envisioned as "a catalyst for the neighbourhood" of El Terreno, in the west of the Mallorcan city, […] 
 The post  OHLAB experiments with colour-blocking and cork in old and new buildings of Terreno Barrio Hotel in Mallorca  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Amy Frearson Editor-at-large 27 October 2026 Photography by Jose Hevia Mallorca-based architecture and interiors studio OHLAB has overseen the design of a hotel in Palma, including a renovated heritage building from 1935 and a new structure built from cross-laminated timber and cork . The 41-room Terreno Barrio Hotel was envisioned as “a catalyst for the neighbourhood” of El Terreno, in the west of the Mallorcan city, serving as a community hub as well as a destination for tourists. Drawings and photographs Close Ground floor plan Section Section concept diagram Floor plan concept diagram “Terreno is not conceived as a tourist object imposed on its context, but as a device for exchange – a hotel that, before being a hotel, aims to be an extension of the barrio,” said OHLAB founders Paloma Hernaiz and Jaime Oliver. “This is not a slogan; it is the principle that orders programme, thresholds, atmospheres and materiality.” The new building stands alongside a renovated heritage block from 1935 The hotel’s reception is in the renovated 1935 building, a five-storey apartment block designed by local architect Francesc Casas, along with the restaurant and bar, a club, and a roof bar. OHLAB refers to this building as “the stage”, the eye-catching focal point of the complex, while the new structure is described as “the bazaar”, its civic heart. Wrapping a new public plaza, this second block houses the community-led spaces, including a cafe, coworking areas, a bookshop and gallery, pop-up retail, a gym, a spa and a cinema. A ramped floor features the same red as the hotel logo OHLAB adopted different strategies for the architecture and interior design of the two structures, creatively exploring the themes of building and material reuse in various ways. “Here, circularity was understood not only as an environmental or material strategy, but also as an economic, social and territorial one, a way of keeping value within the local ecosystem by activating residents, culture, crafts, suppliers and everyday life,” they said. In the renovated building, interior design revives the existing structure rather than covering it. Communal spaces have a theatrical character, with patterned floor tiles and heavy curtains. Highlights include a golden mirror bar and a wool curtain installation by artist Sylvia Sanchez Montoya . A wool curtain installation by Sylvia Sanchez Montoya features in the reception and restaurant OHLAB’s red bar stools front a polished brass bar In the bedrooms, colourblocking creates a horizontal divide between top and bottom. Floors and furniture feature matching terrazzo, produced by local tile manufacturer Huguet using the project’s demolition waste. In the bedrooms, colourblocking divides the rooms into two halves Materials are even more prominent in the seven-storey new building, thanks to the choice of materials. Cork clads the courtyard-facing north facade, while the other exterior walls feature timber louvres that shade the windows from direct sunlight. Inside, the exposed CLT structure is brought to life through more playful use of colour and materials. The cafe and shop is a key example, with shades of brown and lime green extending across to the terrazzo floors and wooden furniture. Bedrooms in the new building feature murals by artist Albert Pinya The bedrooms in this block have a different character, with murals by Mallorcan artist Albert Pinya , bathrooms housed inside mirrored boxes, and timber flooring that merges with joinery. OHLAB was appointed by José Taltavull, who developed the concept for the hotel after being brought on board by hotelier Lydia Piñero. Taltavull appointed graphic design office StudioRoses to oversee the hotel’s visual identity, which fed into OHLAB’s scheme. Various elements were picked out in the same red as the hotel logo, including the ramped floor between the bar and reception, the stage in the club, and the sculptural stools located in the bar. Most of the furniture was either designed by OHLAB or sourced from Mallorca-based manufacturers. A DJ table was made from cork leftover from the construction, while Mallorcan artist Pedro Óliver contributed the neon lighting pieces that feature throughout. StudioRoses designed the hotel’s visual identity, including the logo and signage The new building features flexible co-working, cafe and retail spaces Terreno Barrio Hotel is the latest in a series of major openings in Palma in recent years, with the city in the midst of a cultural renaissance. El Terreno is a major part of that story, particularly since Mallorca-based shoe brand Camper completed its 15,000-square-metre Project Gomila in 2023, which includes the new Jasper Morrison-designed Can Pa bakery . OHLAB’s other projects in the city include the Can Santacilia residential development and the Paral·lel apartment complex . Project credits : Client: Grupo Piñero Concept: José Taltavull Branding and initial brief: José Taltavull, Studio Roses, Joan Alvares Graphic design: Studio Roses Architecture and interior design: OHLAB OHLAB team: Paloma Hernaiz and Jaime Oliver with Robin Harloff, Juan Carlos Martínez, Carlos Garijo, Lara Ortega, Maria Bruna Pisciotta, Sonia Hernan, María Dominguez, Bárbara Beltrán, Elisa Lazzarotto, Pablo Sinan, Loreto Angulo, Marta Carvalho, Wiktoria Krapiec, Camila Ospina, Laura Barros, Sofía Galdame, Maja Stankowska, Mateusz Baranowski, Natalie Battah, Thea Schütz, Zheng Xiagyuan, Izabella Warcaba, Eirini Papadatou, Katerina Rangelova Quantity surveyor: Jorge Ramón Project management: Jorge Ramón, Rafa del Toro Structural engineering: HIMA HVAC/MEP engineering: INGENIO CLT timber structure: Egoin Passive House consultant: Plus Aurea LEED consultant: PGI Acoustic consultant: Tafor, Ambient Acoustics Sound consultant: INTRVL, Ibasa Lighting consultant (club and wool curtain): INTRVL Landscape design: Verdsatile Landscape execution: Amor Photography by Jose Hevia Read more Architecture Interiors

items.title: Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC
items.summary:
Local architecture studio INC has designed each guest room at this hotel overlooking New York's Rockefeller Plaza to emulate "a stateroom on an ocean liner". The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex. For the interiors, INC pulled in […] 
 The post  Luxury ocean liners inform New York's Kimpton Era hotel by INC  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dan Howarth 3 October 2026 Local architecture studio INC has designed each guest room at this hotel overlooking New York ‘s Rockefeller Plaza to emulate “a stateroom on an ocean liner”. The 529-key Kimpton Era is housed within a purpose-built, 33-storey tower on West 48th Street, just south of the art deco Rockefeller Center complex. The Kimpton Era’s blackened-steel staircase spirals up through a three-storey fluted atrium For the interiors, INC pulled in references from New York City itself, blending Uptown elegance and Downtown grit, as well as the compact grandeur of the luxury liners that once docked along the Hudson. “Every detail of the Kimpton Era is engineered elegance with a room that feels more like a stateroom on an ocean liner – compact, crafted, and refined to the luxury of just enough,” said INC partner Adam Rolston. The reception area is anchored by a tiered black-stone counter Materials throughout were chosen to reflect the city’s dichotomy, pairing marbles, brass, leather and glazed ceramics with more industrial concrete and blackened steel. In a triple-height atrium wrapped in fluted concrete, a blackened steel-and-glass stair coils around a mobile of organic forms that descends from the ceiling. The second-floor brasserie featured panelled walls and mosaic flooring Cerused wood, terrazzo borders and diffused lighting define the elevator lobbies, while the tiered black-marble reception counter provides a weighted presence. “Inspired by the city itself, the Kimpton Era captures New York’s layered character — elegant yet gritty, refined yet raw – woven into a vertical voyage of venues and comfort in a purpose-built skyscraper at the heart of Rockefeller Center,” said INC’s Hillary Kroll. Terracotta-toned walls and ceramic pendants add texture in the restaurant spanning the ground and cellar levels The hotel’s five dining venues include a Latin American eatery with terracotta walls and ceramic pendants that spans from the ground floor to the cellar. A second-floor brasserie features banquette seating, panelled walls, a scarlet ceramic bar and mosaic floors, while the third-floor lobby cafe offers coffee in the mornings and cocktails at night. On the roof, a bar references the dining rooms of Chinatown via a tomato-red counter framed by tiled portals, temple-like joinery and hand-painted lotus motifs. The Kimpton Era’s guest rooms are designed like compact ship cabins, with each “berth” featuring full white-oak walls that integrate a bed, desk and storage into a single furniture element. White oak millwork integrates multiple furniture pieces in the guest rooms Neutral colour palettes are offset by jewel-toned fabrics and brass accents, while wet-room-style bathrooms are defined by frosted, blackened metal-framed sliding glass doors that conserve space. “[The Kimpton Era] is a self-contained voyage where guest rooms are like staterooms and lounges, and dining rooms unfold like the salons of a great ocean liner in a new expression of New York luxury,” said INC’s Louisa Revitte. Jewel-toned fabrics enliven the otherwise neutral rooms INC’s previous hotel projects have included the 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge with Marvel Architects, and the event spaces at the TWA Hotel inside Eero Saarinen’s JFK Airport terminal. The studio – which celebrates its 20th anniversary this year – has also completed “gritty yet inviting” interiors for a restaurant in BIG’s The Spiral skyscraper, and filled its own concrete-forward offices with eclectic furniture and plants. The photography is by Read McKendree . Read more Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Raised walkway ties together 360‑metre-long hotel
items.summary:
Chinese studios HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan, China, which is connected by a 360-metre-long raised walkway. Named Dayun Landison Manor, the hotel occupies the elongated site of a demolished village. It stretches 360-metre-long from east to west, with a maximum width of 54 metres in the middle that […] 
 The post  Raised walkway ties together 360‑metre-long hotel  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Kaia Wang 29 September 2026 Chinese studios HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan, China , which is connected by a 360-metre-long raised walkway. Named Dayun Landison Manor, the hotel occupies the elongated site of a demolished village. It stretches 360-metre-long from east to west, with a maximum width of 54 metres in the middle that narrows to 21 metres at the ends. HB Architects and Nature Times Art have completed a hotel in Jiashan The hotel is formed of numerous buildings connected by a walkway raised 4.9 metres above ground. According to the studios, this horizontal layout is a nod to the history of the site and an attempt to recreate a village-like neighbourhood. “We fictionalised a village to continue the functional essence of ‘dwelling’,” HB Architects and Nature Times Art told Dezeen. Terracotta red and earthy yellow are used as the main colours of this building The raised guest rooms were also designed to reference local housing, which is often supported on pilotis. However, the columns supporting the structures were deliberately hidden to highlight the visual dominance of the horizontal slab that runs through the site. The slab is 1.1 metres thick and sits 4.9 metres above the ground The hotel’s entrance opens into a courtyard with a lake at its centre and a “water curtain” that falls from surrounding walkway. Guests then walk up stairs to the raised walkway that passes around courtyards and gardens to get to the rooms. A large pool occupies the tip at one end of the raised platform. “The building offers more than just one kind of experience,” said the studios. “You have to walk through it yourself to really get it.” While the rooms are arranged in blocks surrounding the raised walkway, more functional spaces were placed below the slab. The upper blocks were painted earthy yellow, while the lower floor and walkways were painted terracotta red as a reference to the surrounding landscape. Courtyards allow nature to permeate throughout the building “We deliberately chose to avoid white buildings,” said HB Architects and Nature Times Art. “The colours we use in this building show how we think about nature.” “The main colours relate to our design keywords—’earth’ or ‘nature’,” they continued. The entrance is surrounded by a water curtain HB Architects and Nature Times Art are architecture and interior practices based in Shenzhen. Elsewhere in China, WATG and Wimberly Interiors have completed a boutique hotel in Wuxi’s Dangkou Ancient Town , and BLUE Architecture Studio has transformed a cluster of new and old buildings in Yangzhou into a hotel complex . The photography is by Guowei Liu. Project credits: Client: Jiashan Dayun Cultural Tourism Development Co. Principal Architects: He Bin, Lai Erxun / HB Architects, Wei Jinjing / Nature Time Art Design Team: Zhou Yuxin, Li Wenjing, Liu Ming, Shi Lingli, Fang Xuecen Read more Architecture

items.title: SODA transforms hostel into "design-conscious" pod hotel
items.summary:
London studio SODA has converted a backpacker hostel into Otherwander Soho, a high-density capsule hotel in central London with vibrantly-coloured social spaces. Otherwander combines 566 sleeping pods, or "nests", with shared social spaces, targeted at young travellers and those seeking budget-friendly city-centre accommodation. It occupies a former hostel housed across a pair of early 20th-century […] 
 The post  SODA transforms hostel into "design-conscious" pod hotel  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Lizzie Crook Architecture editor 27 September 2026 London studio SODA has converted a backpacker hostel into Otherwander Soho, a high-density capsule hotel in central London with vibrantly-coloured social spaces. Otherwander combines 566 sleeping pods, or “nests”, with shared social spaces, targeted at young travellers and those seeking budget-friendly city-centre accommodation. It occupies a former hostel housed across a pair of early 20th-century buildings close to Oxford Street, transformed and expanded by SODA . SODA has created the Otherwander capsule hotel in Soho “The aim was to provide affordable, high-density accommodation without compromising the guest experience,” SODA director Ryan Holland told Dezeen. “The original target demographic was primarily Gen Z and younger independent travellers who are design-conscious and prioritise location and experience,” Holland continued. “However, our intention was always to create a design which felt inclusive to all demographics, and we’re now finding that the hotel has a much broader appeal to all sorts of age groups who equally want well-designed, affordable accommodation in central London.” It contains 566 sleeping pods Pod hotels, also known as capsule hotels, are affordable, ultra-compact accommodation comprising rows of small stacked sleeping spaces and shared bathroom and social areas, rather than traditional ensuite rooms. They are often associated with Japan, where the first example opened in Osaka in 1979. They are now becoming increasingly common in cities around the world. Visitors enter through a glossy lobby with e-gates “Pods make central city locations more affordable in a city where space and hotel costs are exceptionally high,” said Holland. “The model particularly suits short stays and travellers who intend to experience the city rather than spend significant time in their room.” Social spaces are located on the ground floor SODA oversaw both the architecture and interiors of the project. It focused on preserving, retaining and connecting the pair of heritage buildings on Dean Street, while adding a rear extension that felt contemporary yet in keeping with the area. The extension replaces what the studio called a “low-quality post-war addition” to the site and primarily houses the hotel’s fully accessible accommodation and facilities, as complex stepped connections were unavoidable in the existing buildings. Its design takes visual cues from nearby brick buildings in Soho, with details including hand-laid arched details and corbelled window reveals. There is a mix of single- and double-bed pods Inside, visitors are welcomed to a glossy, white-walled lobby area called the Gallery, which has a giant digital screen and automated QR-code check-in and e-gates. The QR codes form part of a wider tech-first strategy for the hotel, which means the number of staff is kept to a minimum. This approach was among the features SODA developed through workshops with young people, who offered feedback on how they like to travel and helped the studio “fine-tune the balance between privacy, sociability and automation”. Beyond the Gallery are the ground-floor social spaces, named the Huddle, which has a cocooning feel thanks to a mix of warm colours and materials. This includes pink and green banquette seating and a horseshoe-shaped neon bar. From here, visitors can access the pods either by taking a lift to their floor or by using the five-story staircase that changes in colour as it ascends. The pods occupy the four upper floors as well as the basement, with the bathrooms and supporting facilities distributed across each level. Colour lighting brings a “futuristic atmosphere” to the hotel “This layout developed from the challenge of connecting existing buildings with differing floor levels, while creating clear circulation and keeping guest, public and servicing routes separate,” said Holland. The “nests” are the width of either the single or double bed held inside and arranged in double-stacked bays of four with integrated stairs. Also accessed by QR code, each pod is acoustically isolated and individually ventilated and illuminated. They can be individually serviced and controlled. There are male, female and unisex bathrooms, all fitted with several rain showers and vanity areas. Terrazzo finishes add a contemporary feel that SODA said “exceeds typical traveller expectations”. Terrazzo features in the shared bathrooms A bold use of colour throughout the hotel is designed to add a youthful feel to the interior while also assisting with wayfinding. “Colour lighting effects also create a futuristic atmosphere that shifts in response to the time and mood of the space, from a quiet Tuesday morning to a dynamic Soho Friday night,” said Holland. A colourful staircase links the floors of the hotel Another pod hotel featured on Dezeen is Nine Hours in Shibuya, which was overhauled by Schemata Architects and updated with a suite of timber-lined saunas. Elsewhere, SODA recently converted an Art Deco landmark in London into a contemporary workspace punctuated by a raspberry-red spiral staircase. The photography is by Ruth Ward . items.summary:
Promotion: H World has debuted its latest hotel brand, the Grand Ji Hotel, in Hangzhou, China, designed by Chinese studio Vermilion Zhou Design Group, which aims to reinvent hotel design through its dedication to symbolic ritual. Grand Ji Hotel, a premium brand under H World Group, has made its official debut at Paris Design Week's […] 
 The post  Grand Ji Hotel debuts at Paris Design Week  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dezeen staff 18 September 2026 Promotion: H World has debuted its latest hotel brand, the Grand Ji Hotel, in Hangzhou, China , designed by Chinese studio Vermilion Zhou Design Group, which aims to reinvent hotel design through its dedication to symbolic ritual. Grand Ji Hotel, a premium brand under H World Group , has made its official debut at Paris Design Week’s China Creative Power (CCP) pavilion as an official annual partner, taking place from 10 to 19 September. The hotel’s spatial design was led by Kuang Ming (Ray) Chou, founder and creative director of Vermilion Zhou Design Group and chief designer of H World Group. H World debuted its Grand Ji Hotel during Paris Design Week According to H World, Grand Ji Hotel draws on the phrase “the formless greatness, a quiet way of seeing” and is informed by the Taoist concept of 大象无形, which suggests that the most powerful forms are often “quiet and insular”. Instead of an overtly luxurious look, the hotel’s aesthetic is described as “quiet, yet possessed of presence, unlayered, yet full of depth”. The technology woven into the design ensures the guest experience is seamless Rather than weaving traditional Chinese imagery throughout the hotel design, Grand Ji Hotel was designed to break the conventional hotel paradigms and instead focus on quietly enhancing visitor experience. For example, the way guests arrive, dine, rest and depart are treated as part of one integrated system. When guests arrive, instead of checking in at a large front desk, they are greeted by a tea table where they can first enjoy a tea ceremony and a hot cup of tea. Guests are greeted with a tea ceremony upon arrival At Grand Ji Hotels, technology is integrated purposefully into the background to ensure a smooth experience. Visitors can use their phones as a room key, and rooms are also fitted with innovative control systems, where curtains, televisions, and air conditioning are controlled via voice commands. H World explained that the “Eastern spirit” is woven into each room’s design, with furniture that evokes a sense of sensory calm and hospitality rituals embedded in the structure. H World Group is one of the world’s largest hotel groups Throughout the creative process, the designers also looked to incorporate cultural and natural motifs into the building’s spatial qualities. Here, the materials, art and how light flows through the building were influenced by five Eastern motifs: water, clouds, mountains, pine and tea. Water symbolises the hotel’s flow and calmness, clouds stand for lightness, tea represents zen, mountains signify depth, and pine embodies resilience. The bricks within the hotel entrance wall were made from compressed tea leaves, introducing scent before guests enter the lobby H World explained that its inclusion in Paris Design Week is the first time a Chinese hotel brand has taken part in the week under its own name, which marks a shift from Chinese hotel brands “leading in scale” to “leading in design.” H World added that Grand Ji Hotel’s participation also spotlights the Chinese hotel industry’s growing force within the international design space. Grand Ji Hotel was designed to break with the conventional hotel paradigms and instead focus on enhancing the visitor experience With over 13,000 hotels and more than one million rooms across 21 countries, H World Group is one of the world’s largest hotel groups. The company is headquartered in Shanghai, China, and also offers a portfolio spanning diverse brands, including HanTing Hotel, JI Hotel, Orange Hotel, IntercityHotel, Zleep Hotel, Steigenberger Hotels & Resorts and Steigenberger Icons. To learn more about H World Group, visit its website here . Partnership content This article was written for H World as part of a partnership. Find out more about our partnership content here . items.text: Amy Peacock Architecture reporter 15 September 2026 Hotelier Not A Hotel has revealed its latest guesthouse will take the form of a human-sized Pokémon Poké Ball, nestled beside a lake in Hokkaido , Japan. Set to be built in Tomakomai City, the Poké Ball-Themed Hotel will feature a three-metre-diameter spherical guest room shaped like the balls used to catch and store wild creatures in the popular Pokémon game. Not A Hotel has announced it will open a guest room shaped like a giant Poké Ball Designed by Not A Hotel ‘s in-house team of architects, the structure will comprise two moulded acrylic hemispheres and a curved acrylic window, giving the appearance of an opening ball. It will aim to immerse guests in both the natural setting and the world of Pokémon. It will be situated on a lakeside in Hokkaido Visitors will enter the spherical structure through a sliding, curved door. Inside, a custom-designed circular mattress will fill most of the interior. A washroom will be decorated in tiles the colour of the Snorlax – a Pokémon character known for its long sleeping habits. Guests will be able to select custom interior lighting themes based on Pokémon characters. “As society becomes increasingly convenient and efficient, Not A Hotel aims to bring more joy to individuals’ lives,” said Not A Hotel. “For years, Pokémon fans have dreamed of stepping inside a Poké Ball,” it continued. “Not A Hotel, leveraging its architectural and technological expertise, has turned that dream into a reality.” “This structure transcends the boundaries of architecture and product design, fusing the world of Pokémon with the architectural quality that defines Not A Hotel.” A circular mattress will fill the space Created in collaboration with sleep-tracking game app Pokémon Sleep , the hotel will open in celebration of the third anniversary of Pokémon Sleep and the 30th anniversary of Pokémon this year. Not A Hotel said people will get the chance to stay in the giant poké ball by winning an upcoming competition, but the room will not open to the public for bookings or visits. Other projects by Not A Hotel that have featured on Dezeen include a coastal holiday home designed by Sou Fujimoto and a trio of rammed-earth villas designed by BIG . items.title: Orms plans to add rooftop swimming pool to London's BT Tower
items.summary:
Architecture studio Orms has submitted a planning application to transform the BT Tower in London into a hotel with a rooftop swimming pool for American hotelier MCR. Orms will restore the Grade II-listed BT Tower, the adjacent podium and 1930s Howland Building, and convert the complex into a hotel with ground-floor shops, bars and restaurants, […] 
 The post  Orms plans to add rooftop swimming pool to London's BT Tower  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Amy Peacock Architecture reporter 10 September 2026 Architecture studio Orms has submitted a planning application to transform the BT Tower in London into a hotel with a rooftop swimming pool for American hotelier MCR. Orms will restore the Grade II-listed BT Tower, the adjacent podium and 1930s Howland Building, and convert the complex into a hotel with ground-floor shops, bars and restaurants, if the application is approved by the London Borough of Camden. A publicly accessible swimming pool will be built on top of the podium, which will be overlooked by the iconic BT Tower structure. Orms has submitted a planning application to transform the BT Tower into a hotel with a rooftop swimming pool Plans also include improving the public space around the building and opening the upper portion of the 177-metre-tall tower to the public for the first time since 1981. “Our vision has always been to honour the BT Tower’s remarkable history while reimagining its future,” said MCR CEO Tyler Morse. “Submitting our planning application is an exciting step towards reopening this landmark after almost 50 years, revitalising the area with new jobs and open space for Camden.” Originally designed by the Ministry of Public Building and Works, led by chief architects Eric Bedford and G R Yeats, the communications tower opened in 1964 as the Post Office Tower. Designed to support microwave aerials, which were removed in 2011, the distinctive structure was topped by a revolving restaurant that closed in the early 1980s. The BT Tower was the tallest building in London when it was built and retained the title until the NatWest Tower was built in 1980. MCR first announced its acquisition of the tower in 2024. At the time, UK practice Heatherwick Studio was set to lead the transformation of the building into a hotel. Orms took over the project earlier this year. Works are expected to commence in 2029, once the building has been fully vacated, and MCR plans for the transformation to be completed and open to the public by 2033. Elsewhere in London, the seminal 22 Parkside house by Richard and Su Rogers was handed over from private ownership to the National Trust , and a group of 19th-century dinosaur sculptures at Crystal Palace Park were restored by HTA Design and Donald Insall Associates. The images are by MCR, Orms and Secchi Smith. Read more Architecture News
