With the masks on from doors-opening, here are the official photographs from Hotel Designs’ most unforgettable event yet… Continuing the legacy of The Brit List Awards , the 2026 edition celebrated a decade of championing the best in British and international hotel design and hospitality. Last night, on 5th November, London’s iconic Ministry of Sound opened its doors to the industry’s most creative and influential figures, who traded their usual attire for masks, glamour and a little mystery. Presided over by Hotel Designs Publisher Katy Phillips, Editor Sophie Harper and SPACE Editor Jess Miles ( also the stars of this year’s teaser video ), the evening transformed the venue into a theatrical world of opulence. The night’s headline moment came with the unveiling of the 15 award winners, chosen from more than 250 finalists. Winners were invited to the stage to be crowned and receive their specially designed trophies from EGGER. Also revealed on the evening, The Brit List 2026 book profiles the top 75 interior designers, architects and hoteliers redefining British hospitality. The full list and digital guide are available to explore below. None of this would have been possible without the support and creativity of our incredible sponsors, so here’s a look at the brands who helped make the tenth Brit List Awards a night to remember. Balsan returned as our red carpet partner, unveiling a 2026 entrance carpet in theme of the masquerade. The French carpet specialist has a heritage stretching back almost three centuries. Muraspec joined Informare as event partners, providing 8-foot pieces of masquerade artwork. The wallcovering brand has been designing and manufacturing in the UK since the 1850s. Schlüter-Systems celebrated with us once again as photobooth partner, the company’s 12,000-plus products can be found at Lympstone Manor, The Newt and Raffles at The OWO. Phillip Jeffries was the award partner for The Interior Designer of the Year Award. Our showcase partners brought the glamour: ADA Cosmetics returned for a second year, sending guests home with their signature goody bags filled with Lalique creams, perfumes and body washes. Amtico was back for a second year. The British luxury vinyl tile specialist has been perfecting its craft since the early 1960s. GROHE joined as a first-time sponsor and, as promised, the team were firmly planted on the dancefloor. Hypnos returned with its much-loved super king bed installation near the stage. Every Hypnos mattress is handcrafted in Buckinghamshire, and the brand has been perfecting sleep for more than 120 years. EGGER , our trophy partner, crafted this year’s winners’ trophies from sustainably sourced wood, a lasting reminder of each winner’s accolade. Finally, thank you to Bonfire , who captured the mood, the wins and the dance moves as our videographers for the evening. items.title: Designed to last: the future of hotel design
items.summary:
Hotel Designs  
 Designed to last: the future of hotel design  
  Designed to last: the future of hotel design  
 Sophie Harper .
items.text: Designed to last: the future of hotel design Designed to last: the future of hotel design WORDS BY Sophie Harper November 6, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Designed to last: the future of hotel design At the Egger Showroom in Clerkenwell during London Design Festival, a panel of hospitality design specialists gathered to ask a deceptively simple question: how do you design a hotel that outlasts the moment it was made for? Chaired by Hotel Designs’ Editor Sophie Harper, the discussion brought together Despina Kalapoda of Marriott International, Sarah Williams of Goddard Littlefair and textile designer Emma Shipley . Their answers differed in detail but converged on one idea: what endures is rarely what shouts loudest. For Despina Kalapoda, longevity begins with discipline. Each Marriott brand rests on fixed principles drawn from who its guest is, with room left for local character. “These are things that each brand needs to remain true to,” she said, giving design a thread that survives every change of fashion. The same logic applies to sustainability: build a solid base, refresh the soft finishes, and question whether anything truly needs replacing. In Barcelona, one hotel was obliged to tile over its bathrooms rather than create waste. Considering sustainability at the development stage, she added, is “way more efficient” than waiting for the next renovation. Image credit: Egger Sarah Williams carried the thought from brand to place. A narrative rooted in landscape, architecture and local culture does not date, she argued, because “That’s not based on trend. That is based on the true DNA of the place.” Even the trickiest brief, a space that serves coffee by morning and cocktails by night, is best solved not by compromise but by invention, with people as part of the performance. At the Corinthia London, for example, a single display table turns afternoon tea into evening theatre. “It’s got to involve the people,” she said. Luxury, she added, has yet to embrace recyclable materials, and designers share responsibility for changing that perception. Emma Shipley, whose hand-drawn, nature-inspired collections have sold steadily since 2018, offered the human counterpoint. “Humans have always been inspired by nature, and I’m sure that will always continue, especially in this digital age we’re living in,” she said, adding that handcrafted work will only become more relevant. Textiles, she noted, are also the gentlest way to renew a room. That digital age loomed over the evening’s lightest and most revealing exchange: the humble hotel television. Despina noted waning enthusiasm for in-room screens, while Sarah admitted to a certain resentment, since the TV dictates where the bed, and therefore the view, must go. Her recent treehouse stay, watched over by an Alexa, left her wanting only to escape. Hidden technology, the panel suggested, serves the guest; visible technology too often intrudes. Image credit: Egger None of the panel claimed to know what a hotel room will look like in fifty years, but all were agreed that the answer to what makes lasting design work well lies less in any fixed features and more in how you make people feel in any given space. Build flexibly, stay distinctive, and hold on to the human connection at the heart of hospitality. Trends will pass. The feeling, if it is built well, stays.  Sienna Shipton .
items.text: The Landmark London has redesigned its 48 Marylebone Suites The Landmark London reimagines its Marylebone Suites as a London apartment WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 5, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio The Landmark London reimagines its Marylebone Suites as a London apartment A £3.8 million redesign with Alex Kravetz Design swaps hotel grandeur for a more residential feel, with marble fireplaces, bespoke bars and a palette of blues, taupe and bronze… The Landmark London has unveiled a redesigned collection of 48 Marylebone Suites, marking a new chapter for the five-star hotel. Created in collaboration with architecture studio Alex Kravetz Design (AKD), the spacious suites blend the building’s historic grandeur with a more contemporary, residential style . Image credit: The Landmark The inspiration is the feel of an elegant London apartment. Classic details are balanced with modern touches, and generous living areas, marble-framed fireplaces and bespoke bars make the suites as suited to relaxing and entertaining as to sleeping. A tranquil palette of blues, taupe and neutral shades is layered with warm bronze accents, tailored upholstery and textured wall panelling. Soft lighting runs throughout, from the expansive living rooms to the bedroom retreats, easing the move from day to evening. Image credit: The Landmark The investment, totalling £3.8 million, covers several suite styles. The 60 sqm Marylebone One Bedroom Suite has a separate living room with a statement fireplace, built-in bookcase and workspace. The Marylebone Junior Suite balances architectural detail with plush furnishings, blurring the line between hotel suite and private pied-à-terre. For families and groups, the Marylebone Family Suite pairs two double beds with a large living space and an Italian marble bathroom, with interconnecting rooms available. Amenities include Dyson hair tools, ARGENTUM toiletries, Smart TVs with Sky and a fully stocked bar with Cartwright & Butler treats. Younger guests are catered for with toys, activities and teepees on request, and a warm cookie and milk turndown at bedtime. items.title: HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal

 Pauline Brettell .
items.text: HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal • Hotel Designs HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 5, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio HBA Los Angeles appoints Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal HBA Los Angeles, the flagship studio of the award-winning global hospitality design firm, has announced the appointment of Gianpiero Gaglione as Principal… A respected designer and creative leader with more than 20 years of international experience, Gaglione brings expertise across luxury hospitality, branded residences, restaurants, and mixed-use developments. His appointment further strengthens HBA Los Angeles’ creative capabilities and positions the studio for continued growth. Gaglione joins HBA Los Angeles following more than six years of running his eponymous design practice, where he led a portfolio of hospitality and high-end residential projects defined by tailored interiors, rich materiality, and quiet confidence. His recent collaborations include projects with MGM Resorts, IHG Hotels & Resorts, and Dreamscape Companies. He previously held senior design roles at Kelly Wearstler, Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, and HBA Singapore. “At HBA Los Angeles, we are committed to investing in the next generation of design leadership while building upon the collaborative culture and design excellence that have long defined our studio,” said HBA Los Angeles Partner Kathleen Dauber. “Gianpiero is the right leader to help shape our next chapter. The combination of his creative vision, international experience, and proven leadership makes him exceptionally well-suited to balance creative ambition with the needs of clients and the complexity of hospitality projects.” Throughout his career, Gaglione has contributed to some of the hospitality industry’s most celebrated properties across North America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. His distinguished portfolio includes Santa Monica Proper, Downtown Los Angeles Proper, The Beekman and The Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York, Soho Beach House in Miami Beach, and Rosewood Miramar Beach in Montecito, Calif. Drawing upon his multidisciplinary background in concept development, interior architecture, FF&E design, and project management, Gaglione creates spaces that emphasize craftsmanship, distinctive character, and a strong sense of place. “HBA has an extraordinary legacy in hospitality design, and I’m excited to join the Los Angeles studio at such an important time in its evolution,” said Gaglione. “I’ve always believed the most compelling interiors are those that feel authentic, personal, and enduring rather than driven by trends. I look forward to collaborating with the talented team, bringing new ideas to the design process, and creating environments that are both memorable for guests and meaningful for our clients.” In his new role, Gaglione will help guide the studio’s creative vision, oversee design projects, and mentor emerging talent while strengthening client relationships. items.text: Accor expands Handwritten Collection through new Verdi Hotels partnership • Hotel Designs Accor expands Handwritten Collection through new Verdi Hotels partnership WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 4, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Accor expands Handwritten Collection through new Verdi Hotels partnership Accor and Corinthia Group have launched a strategic collaboration to bring Verdi Hotels to Handwritten Collection… As part of the collaboration, five Verdi hotels in Malta, Portugal and Tunisia will join the Handwritten Collection brand under a franchise agreement from November 2026, with plans to add two further properties in Hungary and the Czech Republic. Verdi Hotels was launched by IHI plc in 2024 as a distinct management platform in the upscale segment, operating independently from th e Corinthia brand , which is positioned in the luxury hotel sector. Through this new collaboration, Verdi’s management platform will benefit from Accor’s global distribution, marketing and loyalty programmes, further strengthening its performance and operating capabilities. Image credit: Verdi Gzira Promenade Designed to bring together characterful independent hotels, Handwritten Collection showcases properties defined by their strong personality and the genuine warmth of their hosts. Since its launch in 2023, the brand has rapidly grown to more than 50 curated hotels in 22 countries, and a pipeline of 58 hotels around the world. Combining the individuality of independent hospitality with the scale, distribution power and growth platform of Accor, the brand is designed to create long-term value for owners and investors. Simon Naudi, CEO of Corinthia Group, said: “We are very pleased to announce this strategic relationship with Accor. While our focus on the global growth of the Corinthia brand remains undiminished and entirely independent, the development of our second brand, Verdi, will now benefit from Accor’s extensive global marketing reach and the strength of its Handwritten Collection.” Paul Pisani, President of Verdi Hotels, added: “We are very much looking forward to this new relationship, which will add value to our Verdi Hotels and give us the opportunity to grow the brand in new and exciting destinations.” image credit: Verdi St. George’s Bay Philippe Bijaoui, Chief Development Officer, Premium, Midscale & Economy brand for Accor in Europe & North Africa, commented: “This strategic partnership with Verdi Hotels marks an important step in our continued growth ambition. By combining the strength of Verdi Hotels’ management platform with Accor’s distribution, loyalty and brand ecosystem, we aim to unlock new opportunities, accelerate growth and create sustainable value for both parties.” The initial Verdi Hotels properties that will join Handwritten Collections include: Verdi Gżira Promenade, Malta – Located on Malta’s Marsamxett Harbour waterfront, Verdi Gżira Promenade is situated along the lively Gżira seafront promenade and a thriving shopping district. The hotel is within easy reach of Malta’s principal business and leisure districts, making it a convenient base for both business and leisure travellers. Verdi St. George’s Bay Marina, Malta – Situated on St. George’s Bay in St Julian’s, the property enjoys a prominent waterfront location overlooking one of Malta’s best-known bays. The hotel is located close to vibrant dining entertainment and commercial areas, while also providing direct access to the Mediterranean coastline. Image credit: Verdi Tunis Beach Resort Verdi Dragonara (formerly Vivaldi Hotel), Malta – Verdi Dragonara looks out across the Dragonara headland toward the open sea, where the coastline turns rocky and the pace slows. It sits just beyond the busiest streets of St Julian’s, so guests enjoy calmer surroundings and stay close to the town’s dining, leisure and business addresses. Formerly the Vivaldi Hotel, Verdi Dragonara adds a new chapter to Verdi Hotels’ presence in Malta. Verdi Tunis Beach Resort, Tunisia – Nestled on the shores of the Côtes de Carthage, the resort sits along the Mediterranean coastline within easy reach of the Tunisian capital. The property combines resort facilities with proximity to the region’s cultural attractions. Verdi Santarém, Portugal – The hotel is situated in the historic city of Santarém, north of Lisbon, and is a perfect gateway to experience Portugal’s Ribatejo region. The property is positioned within a destination known for its cultural heritage, local traditions and accessibility to other destinations in Portugal. items.text: Case Study: switching off with Hypnos at The Grove • Hotel Designs Case Study: switching off with Hypnos at The Grove WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 4, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Case Study: switching off with Hypnos at The Grove Set within 300 acres of Hertfordshire countryside, The Grove offers the sense of a true country escape, withcomfort and attention to detail throughout the resort that continues into a restful night and a refreshed start to the day… The vibrant five-star resort combines 214 stylish rooms and individually designed suites with an award-winning spa, championship golf course, and distinctive restaurants. At a destination offering so many different ways to spend the day, a restful night’s sleep is essential. The Grove has partnered with Hypnos to provide the comfort expected from a five-star stay. With more than 120 years of bedmaking experience, the fifth-generation British bedmaker works closely with hospitality clients around the world, bringing together craftsmanship, comfort and considered material choices. Image credit: The Grove Hotel “At The Grove and Luxury Family Hotels, creating an exceptional guest experience is at the heart of everything we do, and a truly comfortable, restorative night’s sleep is such an important part of that. We are delighted to partner with Hypnos, whose passion for exceptional craftsmanship, comfort and responsibly sourced materials reflects the same values and high standards we hold across our hotels. It’s a partnership we’re very proud of and one that helps us give our guests the quality, comfort, and restful experience they deserve.” – Denise Newson, Group Purchasing Manager The estate balances its rich 18th-century heritage with a relaxed, contemporary personality. Accommodation spans the historic Mansion and modern West Wing, with interiors designed to make the most of the surrounding landscape. Generous windows frame views across the gardens and countryside, while natural tones, tactile fabrics and large-scale artwork give the guestrooms a warm and individual character. Image credit: The Grove Hotel The Grove’s Mansion suites blend antique and contemporary pieces with original Georgian features, including ornate fireplaces, mouldings and curved bay windows. In the West Wing, nature-inspired interiors bring the outdoors in, creating calm and welcoming spaces in which guests can relax. Beds form a natural focal point within the guestrooms. Their generous proportions and inviting presentation reinforce the sense of comfort, helping guests to switch off at the end of the day and wake feeling rested. Image credit: The Grove Hotel The relationship is founded on more than comfort. The Grove’s commitment to protecting the planet and caring for the people within it is reflected in initiatives that champion sustainability, support the local community and invest in the development and wellbeing of its team. This closely aligns with Hypnos’ own focus on people and planet, including its careful consideration of the provenance and performance of the materials used within its beds. Whether guests spend the day on the golf course, unwind at Sequoia spa, explore the woodland trails or enjoy time together in the Walled Garden, a great night’s sleep provides the foundation for the following day. Through its partnership with Hypnos, The Grove ensures that the comfort and attention to detail found throughout the resort continue into a restful night and a refreshed start to the day. items.text: Dezeen Awards 27 October 2026 The results of the interiors public vote for Dezeen Awards 2026 have been announced, with 14 projects selected as winners by Dezeen’s readers. Projects voted as readers’ favourite include a co-working space in Berlin that offers “more than a boring desk” , as well as a “quietly magical” Toronto cafe that provides a family-friendly third place . Also winning this year’s public vote is an office in Kyiv featuring vintage furnishings, artworks, and quirky touches such as leftover paint swatches . Dezeen Awards 2026 public vote winners revealed this week Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble , will reveal all public vote winners this week. The architecture winners were announced yesterday and the design winners will be revealed tomorrow. Readers were invited to choose their favourite projects out of the 392-strong shortlist in this year’s vote. The vote took place between 28 September and 16 October, spanning shortlists in each of Dezeen Awards’ three main category sectors. This year’s interiors category sponsors include Framery and Programa . Top: Banda Agency Office by Ater Architects. Photo by Yevhenii Avramenko. Above: Coworking Spaces at C1 Alexanderplatz-Berlin by Bruzkus Greenberg. Photo by Bruzkus Greenberg All winning interiors projects are listed below, each with a link to a dedicated page on the Dezeen Awards website where you can find an image and more information about the project. The public vote is separate from the main judging process, in which entries are assessed by our panel of industry-leading judges . items.text: Tom Ravenscroft Editor-in-chief 26 September 2026 This week on Dezeen , we revealed the architecture, interiors and design projects in the running to win this year’s Dezeen Awards . Over the week, we announced all the projects shortlisted for this year’s awards, starting with the 152 projects in the running for the 19 architecture project categories on Monday . On Tuesday, we revealed the 112 shortlisted projects in the 14 different interiors project categories before unveiling the shortlisted design projects on Wednesday. Bentley revealed its first electric car this week In London, car brand Bentley revealed its first fully electric car – an SUV named the Torcal. Ahead of its unveiling, we spoke to design director Robin Page about how the car aims to embrace heritage in a “progressive way”. Bugatti unveiled plans for a skyscraper in Miami In the USA, car brand Bugatti revealed plans to build a 60-storey skyscraper in Miami , which would be its first branded residence in the US. Designed by US architecture studio Brandon Haw Architecture with interiors by Yabu Pushelberg , the skyscraper would join other developments by luxury car brands Porsche , Bentley , Mercedes-Benz and Aston Martin in the city. Meta showcased its Muse Charm device At the Meta Connect showcase, the tech company revealed a series of new products including two new pairs of smart glasses . The company also debuted its Muse Charm device , which is a tamagotchi-style AI agent. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” said Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg. “So if you’re not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show it what’s going on around you.” A Peter Zumthor gallery was one of this week’s most popular projects The most popular projects on Dezeen this week include a trio of buildings for a Swiss museum by Peter Zumthor , a charred timber-clad home in Japan , a multi-generational house in Bengaluru . Listen to our journalists talk about the key design and architecture stories of the past seven days on our Dezeen Weekly podcast , which this week focused on Apple’s folding phone. items.text: Dezeen Awards 24 September 2026 Dezeen Awards, in partnership with Trimble , teamed up with content creator Reece Davey to ask this year’s master jury where the future of architecture and design is headed, in this video . In the reel, the jury members (pictured above) were asked for one thing about the future of architecture or design that excited them, as well as trends spotted from this year’s entries. Davey spoke to architects Daniel Libeskind and Aziza Chaouni , as well as architectural designer John Cummins . He also heard from interior designers Jaime Hayon , Julien Sebban and Smita Thomas , alongside designers Jo Barnard and Martin Lotti . View this post on Instagram A post shared by Reece Davey (@houseofdvey) Reece Davey questioned the Dezeen Awards master jury on the future of design and architecture The jury also discussed how representing ideas, sketching, modelling and visualising are changing and the way in which designers work today. For Cummins, product marketing manager at 3D modelling software company Trimble SketchUp , the value of software lies in how easily it allows a designer to move between different stages of a project, from an initial idea to a three-dimensional model and eventually a finished building. “Software should not be another problem that the designer has to solve,” said Cummins. “SketchUp has always been about giving architects the tools to seamlessly take a project from an idea to a finished building,” he later added. The jury met earlier this month at the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel in London to decide the winners of Dezeen Awards 2026, which will be revealed at this year’s party on 16 November. This week, Dezeen revealed all shortlisted projects in the running for this year’s awards. The architecture shortlist was announced on Monday, followed by the interiors shortlist on Tuesday and the design shortlist yesterday. Next week, the 2026 public vote will open and readers will be asked to vote for their favourite shortlisted projects. We will announce the public vote winners on Dezeen and across our social media channels ahead of the Dezeen Awards party on 16 November. Buy your Dezeen Awards party tickets now! items.text: Dezeen Awards 22 September 2026 Dezeen has announced the interiors shortlist for this year’s Dezeen Awards , which includes projects by Isern Serra , Snøhetta and YSG . The 112 shortlisted projects, which are in the running for awards in 14 different interiors project categories, are by studios located across 26 different countries, including Brazil , Czech Republic , Hong Kong , Kazakhstan , Spain and the United States . Shortlisted projects include an over-century-old dockside warehouse conversion in Scotland, an apartment defined by chamfered surfaces, warm hues and reinstated art deco features in Australia and an old sailor’s home that pays homage to its heritage in Spain. items.text: Chater Paul Jordan 17 September 2026 Fifteen leading architects and designers met last week to decide the winners of Dezeen Awards 2026, in partnership with Trimble , which will be revealed at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party in November. The master jury took place at the One Hundred Shoreditch hotel in London and included architects Ma Yansong and Daniel Libeskind as well as interior designers Wendy Saunders and Jaime Hayon . Designers Martin Lotti and Jo Barnard , as well as architects Dominique Petit-Frère and Aziza Chaouni also joined to determine the 49 winning projects, ahead of next week’s shortlist announcements between 21-23 September. Winners announced at the Royal Opera House All this year’s winners will be announced at the Dezeen Awards 2026 party which takes place at the Royal Opera House in London on 16 November. Guests at the party will be the first to find out who has won the prestigious project of the year awards across architecture, interiors and design. Tickets are available to purchase here . Also unveiled at the ceremony will be the six winners of this year’s Designers of the Year, who have each been shortlisted and selected by Dezeen’s editorial team. The Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design. “Designers thinking more critically about context” The master jury discussed 392 shortlisted entries selected from over 4,300 projects in 91 countries around the globe. Architectural designer John Cummins joined the architecture master jury panel which comprised architects Yansong , Libeskind , Chaouni and Petit-Frère . Speaking to Dezeen, Petit-Frère observed how “this year’s projects reflect a generation of designers thinking more critically about context, materiality, technology, and the social impact of what they create”. Top image: (from left to right) John Cummins, Dominique Petit-Frère, Daniel Libeskind, Ma Yansong and Aziza Chaouni. Above: (from left to right) Wendy Saunders, Jaime Hayon, Smita Thomas, Benni Allan and Julien Sebban at the master jury day at One Hundred Shoreditch Hayon and Saunders were joined on the interiors master jury panel by Benni Allan , Julien Sebban and Bangalore-based Smita Thomas . Thomas was also struck by the depth of this year’s entries, which she saw as imbued with a sense of purpose rather than being solely aesthetic exercises. “There were a number of projects that felt more like statements of intent than displays of style,” she said. “It charged me to see design beginning to shapeshift toward strengthening human connection in a time when we need it most,” Thomas continued. Parisian designer Sebban noted the “presence of so many young and emerging studios experimenting with new materials and new ways of thinking”. “The next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers” Lotti and Barnard were alongside Michael Anastassiades , Min Chen and Alexie Sommer to decide the winners of the design categories. Lotti, chief design officer at sportswear brand Nike , remarked that “the strongest projects weren’t simply beautiful – they were purposeful, distinct and challenging the status quo”. “What struck me most was the range of thinking behind it. I came away feeling that the next generation is asking better questions, not just creating better answers,” he continued. (From left to right) Alexie Sommer, Min Chen, Michael Anastassiades, Jo Barnard and Martin Lotti at the master jury day in London Following the day of judging, an exclusive drinks reception and dinner took place in the One Hundred Room at One Hundred Shoreditch, where the master jury was joined by fellow 2026 judges Zandra Rhodes and Miminat Shodeinde . Designers Paul Cocksedge , Ron Arad and Sebastian Cox also joined to celebrate the day’s conclusion. Following the shortlist announcements next week, the Dezeen Awards 2026 public vote will open and readers will be asked to vote for their favourite shortlisted projects. We will announce the public vote winners on Dezeen and across our social media channels ahead of the Dezeen Awards party on 16 November. Zandra Rhodes and Paul Cocksedge joined for the celebratory dinner at One Hundred Shoreditch. Photo by Olivia Chenery Tickets for the Dezeen Awards 2026 party are on sale. The occasion is an opportunity to celebrate with fellow nominees and VIPs, connect with others from around the world and reward your team for their hard work. Studios that have been shortlisted for this year’s Dezeen Awards will be eligible to purchase discounted tickets for £249. These tickets will be released on 21 September, alongside the shortlist announcements. Subscribe to the Dezeen Awards newsletter to keep up to date with the latest announcements on the party. items.text: Chater Paul Jordan 1 June 2026 British architect Norman Foster is the latest industry leader to be announced as a member of the judging panel for Dezeen Awards 2026 . Dezeen Awards, in partnership with Trimble , is searching for the world’s best architecture, interiors and design. The search finally concludes this coming Wednesday, 3 June at 23:59 London time – there will be no extension to the deadline . Read on for more as “the most successful architect in history” joins this year’s panel. Foster to judge Dezeen Awards 2026 Foster, whose career spans nearly six decades, is renowned as one of the industry’s most prolific names. He leads international studio Foster + Partners, which he founded in 1967, and is behind some of the most notable projects in the world. The architect’s oeuvre reflects his impact as a pioneer and proponent of high-tech architecture . Norman Foster will judge Dezeen Awards 2026 Landmark projects include the HSBC Building in Hong Kong , London Stansted Airport and Apple Park, USA . In an interview with Dezeen, Foster expanded on the importance of “architecture without architects” , advocating for the lessons the industry can take from using buildings constructed with local materials and with passive design strategies. Last year, on the eve of his 90th birthday, Dezeen explored how the Manchester-born architect grew to become the most successful architect in history , speaking to former colleagues and industry peers – including Foster himself. Still highly prolific, he remains at the helm of the global architectural powerhouse as executive chairman, while also serving as president of the Norman Foster Foundation – an initiative that promotes interdisciplinary thinking and research to help new generations of architects, designers and urbanists anticipate the future. Recent projects by Foster + Partners include an art gallery wrapped in with ribbed glass facades , a supertall skyscraper in Manhattan and a museum signalled by soaring ventilation towers modelled on the wings of a falcon . Other projects include a bespoke time capsule created to mark the USA’s 250th anniversary of independence . It will be buried under the plaza at Washington Monument and is destined to be reopened on 4th July 2276 for the USA ‘s 500th Independence Day. Foster is the latest judge to be announced as part of this year’s Dezeen Awards judging panel. He will join the architecture panel alongside Daniel Libeskind , Massimiliano Fuksas and Amanda Levete as well as Malini Doshi , Dominique Petit-Frère and Annabelle Selldorf . Read on to find out more about who will be judging this year’s entries: Julien Sebban will join this year’s interiors panel Sebban is the founder and creative director of Paris -based multidisciplinary design collective Uchronia . He brings his signature bold and joyful approach to immersive projects spanning restaurants, retail spaces, private residences, boutique hotels and monumental installations. Sebban’s practice aims to blur the boundaries between architecture, interior design, scenography and collectible furniture. Recent projects include a hotel suite with an underwater feel , a playful installation at Coachella and a psychedelic revamp of a womenswear boutique . In 2023, Uchronia was named Dezeen Awards emerging interior designer of the year . Natasha Jen will judge this year’s design entries Jen is a multidisciplinary designer and partner at the global branding studio Pentagram . The New York -based graphic designer’s work explores the overlap between technology, contemporary culture and the built environment through graphic identity across physical and digital contexts. Jen has worked on projects for institutions including the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Harvard GSD , as well as architecture practices BIG , OMA and Weiss/Manfredi . An internationally recognised and acclaimed practitioner, she was awarded an honorary fellowship by the Royal College of Arts for her contributions and achievements in the industry. Gabriella Khalil will join the Dezeen Awards 2026 interiors jury Khalil is a creative director, designer and curator known for her immersive approach to design, hospitality and cultural programming. She is the co-founder of Palm Heights , Grand Cayman’s first boutique hotel, and is the creative director at WSA, a New York City -based workspace and event hub. Khalil aims to merge beauty, cultural resonance and human connection in her work, creating spaces that feel both elevated and deeply connected. John Cummins will judge Dezeen Awards 2026 Cummins is an architectural designer and product marketing manager at 3D modelling software brand Trimble SketchUp . He advocates for technology-as-facilitator to help build space for designers to spend time on the human decisions to create meaningful and inspiring built environments. Drawing on his architectural experience, the designer now works closely with some of the largest architecture, engineering and construction firms around the world to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings. items.title: Introducing New York’s 2026 Eater Award Winners
items.summary: This year’s New York City restaurant award winners have a point of view, and they’re sticking to it. Their menus tell a story about where the chefs grew up, who trained them, and how they like to cook. Some give a familiar kind of restaurant a fresh reason to exist; others bring together ingredients you […]
items.text: Dining Out in NY Introducing New York’s 2026 Eater Award Winners The Best New Restaurant, Best New Bakery, Dish of the Year, and more by Nat Belkov , Nadia Chaudhury , Bettina Makalintal , and Melissa McCart Nov 10, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC Facebook Link A spread of dishes from Somssi. | Cole Saladino /Eater NY Facebook Link This year’s New York City restaurant award winners have a point of view, and they’re sticking to it. Their menus tell a story about where the chefs grew up, who trained them, and how they like to cook. Some give a familiar kind of restaurant a fresh reason to exist; others bring together ingredients you might not expect to share a menu. These new restaurants also gave us reasons to keep going out in a year when everything got more expensive. Not every pick here is a bargain, but they’re generous in how you’re treated, what’s on the plate, and often what you’re paying for. These restaurants make dinner feel like a good use of time and money. In New York right now, that’s everything. Without further ado, here are the 2026 selections, and don’t miss the rest of the 2026 Eater Awards , presented by Capital One. Related Check out the map of New York’s 2026 Eater Award winners — and discover special dining perks with select restaurants The Potato Potato Potato at Somssi. Cole Saladino /Eater NY Best New Restaurant: Somssi Somssi , from Ahris Kim and chef Daniel Gronert, is one of the clearest examples in New York of a restaurant that goes all-in on personal history, rather than focusing on the broader food culture of any one country or a region. Korea-born Kim, who ran operations at Atomix , lived in Indonesia and the Philippines before moving to Wisconsin with her family. Gronert, who has German roots and spent time as a pitmaster in South Carolina, cooked across restaurants in Atomix’s parent company. Those influences show up in dishes like the caviar-crowned Potato Potato Potato, a crispy-soft tater tot simulacrum nested on miso hollandaise; ox tongue grilled and glazed with tare, a kaleidoscope of textures; and pork schnitzel presented like shrimp toast (it works). With the team’s fine dining pedigree, Somssi sets a high bar for hospitality, yet it’s still casual: The room is designed to feel like a home, and the menu nods to places Kim and Gronert have lived. The bar extends that expertise. Christian Gray’s cocktails include well-made minis, which the bartenders are game to explain to curious drinkers. Sommelier (and Punch contributor) Jenny Eagleton’s list of wines and sakes leans toward lesser-known areas. The duo and their staff reward handing your night over to them, whether you’re there with a group or alone with a Kindle. Personal touches carry through the space in gloriously analog fashion. Lace curtains on the door spell out the restaurant’s name in embroidery, and handprints line the bathroom wall, left by the broader constellation of people who helped build Somssi into the singular restaurant it is today. — Nadia Chaudhury , deputy editor, Eater New York Fried boca negra at Zoli. Zoli Chef of the Year: Ned Baldwin, Zoli Chef Ned Baldwin has spent more than a decade winning over diners at Houseman in Hudson Square: His restaurant has become the kind of neighborhood fixture any chef would wish to run. Among its regulars are contemporary art center founders, Lonti Ebers and her husband, Bruce Flatt, of Amant : The couple later recruited Baldwin to open Zoli , adjacent to their gallery, after watching him steer Houseman through thick and thin. It was a smart pick. Without fine dining fussiness, Baldwin glams up pole beans with a soy-pickling, he roasts okra for skewers, and he tucks Sungolds with romano beans to make a case for ordering well beyond the fish offerings he’s known for. Still, don’t skip the surf clams with avocado and serrano or the triggerfish with leeks — or really any seafood on the menu, particularly fish Baldwin has caught himself out East. Baldwin’s strength extends to the people cooking alongside him. A generous mentor, he brought Houseman pastry chef Nicole Sheets to Zoli to offer a bigger kitchen and better tools. His restaurant has become a next step for chefs who used to work at standouts like Frenchette, Wildair, and Estela. Baldwin’s achievement here is bigger than a handful of excellent dishes: With his team and his benefactors, he has built a compelling restaurant destination that gives his team room to grow. — Melissa McCart , dining editorial manager Lamb and rib-eye samosa, Saffron Shah, firni concha, and sheer pira. The pastries from Diljān traverse Afghanistan with some Latin American influences. Cole Saladino /Eater NY Best New Bakery: Diljān With Afghan influences and some Latin American flair, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights. Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned with toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — NC The $32 half bird at Badaboom. Henry Hargreaves/Eater Dish of the Year: Badaboom In 2026, one marriage took the food zeitgeist by storm: a holy union between the natural wine bar and roast chicken. The once-casual dinner has been made chic and, increasin

The new restaurant puts cocktails and dinner at the center of the former all-day spot, with […]
items.text: NYC Restaurant Openings Bar Cosme From Enrique Olvera Opens Tomorrow With a Focus on Tortillas The restaurant in the former Atla space opens with fresh-pressed tortillas and cocktails from an Eleven Madison Park veteran by Melissa McCart Nov 9, 2026, 10:08 PM UTC Facebook Link Beet tiradito, lamb chops, and broccolini. | Victoria Martinez Melissa McCart is the lead editor of the Northeast region with more than 20 years of experience as a reporter, critic, editor, and cookbook author. Facebook Link While Enrique Olvera closed Atla in May, he didn’t give up the space: In its place, on Tuesday, November 10, the chef behind Cosme and Mexico City’s Pujol opens Bar Cosme at 11 Great Jones Street, at Lafayette Street. The new restaurant puts cocktails and dinner at the center of the former all-day spot, with drinks from a veteran of Eleven Madison Park and Clemente Bar, and a kitchen built around fresh-pressed tortillas. The comal — the griddle used for cooking tortillas — is central to Bar Cosme. Mexico City architecture studio Taller ADG redesigned the space with stainless steel, walnut, and black granite, including a sculptural central bar. The 40 seats are arranged around the open kitchen and comal, with floor-to-ceiling windows looking onto the corner. The comal at Bar Cosme. Evan Sung/Bar Cosme The menu is organized by seafood and crudo, like oysters with jicama, lime, and charred habanero peppers; meats with dishes like lamb belly seasoned with chintextle, a Oaxacan chile paste; vegetables and sides such as a roasted onion in salsa macha; and sweets like a guava tart. Every order arrives with fresh-pressed tortillas and salsas. In addition to a la carte, there’s a prix fixe for $135, which includes seafood, meat, a side, and dessert. Agave spirits anchor the bar, alongside a selection of bourbons. The cocktail menu is divided between “de la casa,” which are variations on familiar cocktails, and “de la barra,” original drinks from the team. The Lestat combines mezcal, corn liqueur, passion fruit, and elote salt, while the Genevieve takes a savory approach to a martini with Mexican gin, blanco tequila, and mole blanco. There’s also a sparkling highball with plantain and shiso. A 50-bottle wine list includes Mexican and natural wines. Four cocktails: Highball, Genevieve, Silas, and Lestat Victoria Martinez/Bar Cosme The drinks were developed by Sebastian Tollius and Jorsand Diaz. Tollius spent seven years at Eleven Madison Park and helped launch its upstairs Clemente Bar in 2024. Jorsand Diaz, who started as a Cosme bartender, is now the beverage director for the restaurant’s parent group, Casamata . Olvera opened Cosme in Flatiron in 2014 with Daniela Soto-Innes leading the kitchen, establishing a New York destination for contemporary Mexican cooking. In 2017, Cosme debuted on the World’s 50 Best Restaurants list at No. 40, joining Olvera’s Pujol in the top 50. That same year, the pair opened Atla, a more casual restaurant where diners could stop in for breakfast, aguachiles, or a lobster burrito. She left the group in 2020. The shift to Bar Cosme follows nearly nine years of Atla, since it opened in 2017. It became a neighborhood fixture and a comparatively less expensive introduction to Olvera’s cooking than Cosme, earning two stars from then- New York Times critic Pete Wells. Former Eater critic Ryan Sutton was a regular, too: “I’ve probably been back to Atla more than any other restaurant I’ve reviewed in the past year,” he wrote in 2018. Bar Cosme will be open nightly from 5 p.m. to midnight, with reservations through Resy for seatings from 5 to 9 p.m. Limited seating is held for walk-ins. Bar Cosme 372 Lafayette Street, New York, New York 10012, United States Link https://www.instagram.com/barcosmenyc/ See More : NYC Restaurant Openings

Guests at booths place their orders on a giant […]
items.text: NYC Restaurant News A Behemoth Conveyor Belt Sushi Restaurant Descends Upon Times Square ﻿Sushiro touches down in America this month by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 9, 2026, 7:43 PM UTC Facebook Link A Sushiro in Tokyo. Bloomberg via Getty Images Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. Japan’s popular conveyor belt sushi restaurant, Sushiro , is making its American debut in New York City on Thursday, November 19, in Times Square at 667 Eighth Avenue, at West 42nd Street. Sushiro is all about kaiten sushi, aka affordable sushi rolling around on a conveyor belt. Guests at booths place their orders on a giant digital screen, and items from nigiri to tempura to ramen to desserts to sake get delivered to their tables through an intricate conveyor belt system winding throughout the space. Expect to pay $5 to $6 for most sushi pieces, and anywhere from $8 to $10 for fancier ones. People can also earn prizes by playing digital games at their tables. The New York City restaurant is huge, at 9,000 square feet. The first two floors feature 146 seats for a la carte conveyor belt dining. The lower cellar floor is dedicated to private group dining for reservations only with prix fixe menus. Sushiro started in Osaka in 1984 and grew to over 1,000 restaurants around the world under its parent group, Food & Life Companies. New York’s other Japan-based conveyor sushi belt chain, Kura Sushi, operates a location out in Flushing. Sushiro’s New York hours are from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. daily. items.summary: An alum of notable New York City Persian restaurants like Sofreh and Eyval is opening up his own fast-casual restaurant dedicated to Persian wraps. Chef Soroosh Golbabae is opening Āzar in Williamsburg at 740 Driggs Avenue, at South Second Street, on Saturday, November 7.  Golbabae is focusing on the idea of loghmeh, a Persian word […]
items.text: NYC Restaurant News A Sofreh Alum Showcases Persian Wraps in Brooklyn ﻿Chef Soroosh Golbabae debuts Āzar in Williamsburg this weekend by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 6, 2026, 6:35 PM UTC Facebook Link Noah Fecks Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. An alum of notable New York City Persian restaurants like Sofreh and Eyval is opening up his own fast-casual restaurant dedicated to Persian wraps. Chef Soroosh Golbabae is opening Āzar in Williamsburg at 740 Driggs Avenue, at South Second Street, on Saturday, November 7. Golbabae is focusing on the idea of loghmeh, a Persian word that means “morsel” or “perfect bite.” He explains, “Loghmeh is a super-easy homey concept that never made it out of the home,” and he’s doing something about that. To that end, Āzar is serving lavash flatbread wraps with Persian fillings that aren’t overly huge. His version of the Iranian home dining staple ghormeh sabzi ($12) is made with beef cheeks instead of the typical lamb. “Beef cheeks are a favorite cut, and it’s really hot right now, so let’s try it,” he says. It’s cooked in a herby stew with kidney beans and black limes, “until the herbs are really incorporated with all that meat flavor,” he adds, and is garnished with fresh white onions. The food spread at Āzar. Noah Fecks Soroosh Golbabae at Āzar. Noah Fecks Then there’s the koobideh ($12), with a mixture of grilled ground lamb and beef made with saffron butter, plus sumac onions, grilled tomatoes, and fresh basil. The chicken fesenjoon ($9) will be on the menu through the spring; it’s a bright filling with a pomegranate-walnut sauce, grilled chicken thighs, and pickled red cabbage. The vegetarian option is the kashk bademjoon ($9) — a “super-comforting eggplant dish,” he says. “To me, it’s the umami of Persian cuisine.” It’s made with a slow-cooked eggplant, kashk (Persian whey) , and crispy onions. He made his own lavash recipe with some whole wheat flour to add structure, as well as butter “to make it more delicious, more aromatic, and, when it reheats or holds the food, it adds a little more strength.” It’s baked in the on-site pita oven. Golbabae had been working on the idea for some time; “ Āzar is on the back burner, cooking for a long time,” he tells Eater. He knew the name from the beginning, after his mother. He grew up in Tehran, watching his mother shop and cook. “I had that education growing up without even understanding it in the beginning,” he says. The zereshk tanchin at Āzar. Noah Fecks The doogh drink at Āzar. Noah Fecks Look for sides like the tahchin ($8), a smaller take on the iconic Persian rice dish. He shares that he’s generally particular about tahchin. For this one, he went for a “softer, jasmine-like rice; we overcook it intentionally to get a little mushy,” he says. It gets seasoned with yogurt, egg yolks, saffron, and salt “so it becomes really nice and moist and fatty — kind of sticky.” While it’s typically stuffed with meat, vegetables, or barberries, he opted to serve it with the zereshk sauce (made with barberries and prunes) and pistachios for that cold-hot temperature combination. “Two things I really like to play with when I’m coming up with dishes are temperature and texture,” he says. “If you can get a few things in one bite, it’s just amazing; it’s a unique experience.” Drinks include saffron sharbat ($5), made with basil seeds and lime (“super-refreshing, he describes); and doogh ($5), the yogurt drink with dry mint and rose that gets steeped overnight. Growing up in Tehran, Golbabae frequented local street carts, kebab shops, and restaurants, and eventually worked at a few places. He worked there for a bit, and then moved to New York City to attend the Culinary Institute of America, but he wanted to go back to learning more about Persian cuisine. “I started digging [into all the old Persian recipes, thinking about how we can do that, how we can dress it in a different way that New York likes and also not lose the authenticity of it,” he says. That’s when he ended up on the opening team of Prospect Heights restaurant Sofreh (which opened in 2018) and Bushwick’s Eyval ; and then he was the opening chef and chef de cuisine of Park Slope Lebanese restaurant Sawa . He also ran Persian pop-ups and worked as a private chef. All the while, he knew that the Persian community was looking for restaurants that were more accessible and affordable. “In a lot of restaurants nowadays, in many different cuisines, they are inspired by street food, but by the time the food goes on the table, to me, it’s not anymore because they played with it too much — I’m guilty myself — but I was like, maybe this is the time to take a little risk and come out of that comfort zone,” he explains. He met Fardad Zabetian, who founded Kudo , a live-translation program, during a pop-up, and they teamed up to open Āzar. Āzar’s dining room. Noah Fecks Āzar’s exterior. Noah Fecks The 350-square-foot counter-service space is small, with only 10 seats. It’s designed by architecture firm Roudiani.Harelson . Golbabae talks about how the firm’s co-founder, Bahar Roudiani, immediately understood his Iranian architectural references because she lived in Iran. He’d ask her about old houses in Iran and stainless steel details in the Albanian sandwich shops, and she knew them all. For Āzar, that means a stainless steel counter and amber glass blocks. The walls feature artwork by fellow Iranians and Iranian Americans. Sina Choopani, who runs Tehran-based silk-screen print studio Garage.co , has some silk prints up. Zeynab Izadyar, the founder of Vvork Vvork Vvork , has patched-together quilts. items.text: NYC Restaurant News Bark Barbecue’s Brooklyn Food Hall Run Is Done ﻿Plus, a short-lived omurice pop-up — and more restaurant shutters by Tierney Plumb Nov 6, 2026, 5:32 PM UTC Facebook Link Barbecue and sides at Bark barbecue. Tierney Plumb is an editor of Eater’s Northeast region, covering D.C., Boston, Philly, and New York. This is Eater’s guide to all the New York City restaurants, bars, and cafes that closed in November 2026. This list will be updated weekly (see: October , September , August , July , June , May , April , March , February , January ), serving as a round-up of the dining and drinking places that have shuttered around the city. If a restaurant or bar has closed in your neighborhood, let us know at ny@eater.com. November 6 Spotlight Dumbo : After three years, Bark Barbecue will close its first-ever permanent outpost inside Brooklyn’s Time Out Market on Saturday, November 7. “All good things must come to an end,” its cowboy hat-wearing pitmaster Ruben Santana tells followers in a video message near his walk-up food hall stall. But luckily, fans of his Central Texan barbecue with Dominican touches don’t have to go far to find white oak-smoked brisket, ribs, pulled pork, and plenty of sides. Bark’s huge Bushwick location, complete with 1,000-gallon smokers, opened this summer to much excitement. However, the space will get a new tenant soon. Per EV Grieve , there’s a recently approved application for a to-be-named tavern to slide in and take over. items.text: NYC Restaurant News ICYMI: A Portuguese Bakery Spins Off a New Soft Serve Shop And more New York City restaurant intel to know this week by Nadia Chaudhury Nov 6, 2026, 3:02 PM UTC Facebook Link Soft serve at Lisbonata. Lisbonata Nadia Chaudhury is a born-and-raised New Yorker who is the deputy editor for Eater’s Northeast region and Eater New York, was the former Eater Austin editor for 10 years, and often writes about food and pop culture. We’ve been covering various NYC restaurants, food, drinks, bars, etc. news intel over on our daily newsletter ( please sign up if you haven’t already! ), but we’re also making it easier for everyone to catch up by rounding ‘em up here every week (check out October , September , August , July , and June’s ). November 6 Soft serve > fro-yo (!?!) Looks like Crown Heights Portuguese bakery Lisbonata is opening a spinoff location focused on its soft serve , Sofi , in the West Village, at 31 Carmine Street, between Bedford and Bleecker streets. Eater has reached out for more information. Why a chef left a hyped art museum restaurant The New Museum’s new restaurant Oberon opened in July on the Lower East Side, by the Oberon Group (which runs places like Rhodora , June , and Rucola ) with co-executive chefs artist Julia Sherman and Ali Ghriskey. But then, less than a month later, Sherman left the operation. In her Substack newsletter, Salad for President , on Friday, October 30, she explained what happened behind the paywall, calling it an “ultimate failure to launch.” She recounts how the owner told her, “food doesn’t matter,” and that she wasn’t supposed to talk about the restaurant in the press. An omurice pop-up shutter That was quick: Osaka, Japan-based omurice-slinging restaurant Dearbros already closed its nine-day-old pop-up at Japanese cafe BentOn on Thursday, October 29, because they were overwhelmed with guests. They’re turning their attention to opening a permanent New York City restaurant. Eater has reached out for more information. A ramen restaurant returns One of Brooklyn’s earlier ramen slingers, Chuko Ramen , closed its 15-year-old Prospect Heights location over the summer. But it turns out the team is reopening the restaurant on the border of Clinton Hill and Bed-Stuy at 395 Classon Avenue, at Greene Avenue, in January 2027. New NYC food and drink book alerts First, Ayesha Nurdjaja , the chef and partner behind NYC restaurants Shuka and Shukette , published her first cookbook, Mediterranean All the Way . And then, drinks-focused writer Robert Simonson ’s latest, Bourbon & Rye Cocktails . “Music for a pizza restaurant” Harry Styles ended his record-breaking 30-show residency at Madison Square Garden at the end of October, and he celebrated with food, of course. For his final show on Halloween, aka Harryween, he dressed up as a full-on pizza rat, a reference to his first-night banter about how much he loves grabbing a late-night slice when he’s in NYC, and switched to the rat ears and a white shirt declaring “I am a rat.” That’s when he and his band ate pizza from Williamsburg Pizza on stage, per Yes Williamsburg . Continuing the theme, his girlfriend, Zoë Kravitz, dressed up as a plastic takeout bag . “I just wanna taste it” Earlier during the residency, Styles celebrated the birthday of one of his fans at the show with a cake from East Village bakery From Lucie . Political dining out NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani spent his Halloween touring the final night of the Queens Night Market with New York City Governor Kathy Hochul, who had been up for reelection that week and won. Learn about an acclaimed winemaker There’s a new documentary about renowned California winemaker Randall Grahm from director Jeffrey Reiner and producer Darin Bresnitz coming out this fall called The Terroirist . They’re hosting a preview screening on Monday, November 9, at the Loft at City Winery in Chelsea starting at 7 p.m., with a discussion between Grahm, Reiner, and moderator/winemaker/sommelier André Hueston Mack, plus wines from Grahm’s vineyard, for $36. The documentary premieres on streaming services such as Apple TV and Amazon Prime on Friday, November 13. items.text: Dining Out in LA Introducing LA’s 2026 Eater Award Winners The Best New Restaurant, Chef of the Year, Dish of the Year, and more by Nicole Fellah , Rebecca Roland , Matthew Kang , Mona Holmes , and Hilary Pollack Nov 10, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Tlayudas from Lugya’h at Maydan Market. | Stan Lee/Eater Facebook Link A slew of reimagined bistros , revivals of old dining favorites , colorful cafes, and specialty pastry makers all entered the Los Angeles scene this past year and struck a chord with diners. But being a successful Los Angeles restaurant in 2026 meant far more than superlative food and service. Each introduced experiences that transcend what we expect from a restaurant in spite of a severe economic slowdown , continuing ICE raids , and a steep decline in Los Angeles tourism . This crop of restaurants reflects the continued inventiveness of Los Angeles’s chefs and independent business owners in the face of uncertainty. In late 2025, Little Fish expanded into Melrose Hill, drawing crowds with a unique style of West Coast seafood, while Hermon’s became an envied neighborhood restaurant. Yerord Mas’s $38 sandwich kept long lines, while tasting menu prices dropped considerably. The year 2026 was also one of rebirths, with chef Ray Garcia’s Broken Spanish Comedor , chef Casey Lane’s formidable Tasting Kitchen , and the return of classic movie palaces . Those looking for inventive wine bars and cocktails found newcomers like Bar Betsy and Vandell , the latter with its clever produce-focused drinks. Of course, awarding the best of the new also becomes a bittersweet acknowledgement as longtime favorites like Taix , Crustacean , and Sky’s Gourmet Tacos shuttered in 2026. Though plenty of predictable “ Erewhonified ” restaurants debuted, refreshing bakeries like Pinecone also emerged, as did Pasadena’s cinnamon roll expert Badash Bakes . The taco scene continues to deliciously veer Northern Mexican, with styles from Tijuana and Sonora gaining influence at Echo Park’s Tijuanero by Tijuanazo and Silver Lake’s carne asada superstar, Tacos Royale . Here are the 2026 Eater Award winners, representing the best and brightest of the newcomers in Los Angeles of the past year. Visit Eater for the full list of 2026 Eater Awards , presented by Capital One. — Mona Holmes , editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest Related Check out the map of LA’s 2026 Eater Award winners — and discover special dining perks with select restaurants Alfonso Martinez. Stan Lee/Eater Tlayudas and meat on the grill at Maydan Market. Stan Lee/Eater Best New Restaurant: Maydan Market Maydan Market opened in 2025 as a collaborative restaurant space and marketplace home to a few different Los Angeles-born businesses; in essence, it functions as one super-incubator for some of the best food you can find in the city. Diners bounce around to try a pozole flight and pescadillas (sofrito-fried fish nested in supple blue corn tortillas) at Maléna, from the family behind the beloved Tamales Elena; a crisp, UFO-sized, asiento-painted tlayuda from Lugya’h, from Los Angeles legend Poncho’s Tlayudas; and chile-sauce-slicked gai tod from Golden Mountain Chicken (formerly Yhing Yhang), from the intrepid team behind Thai restaurant Holy Basil. They will certainly stop to perch at the rotating Club 104 stall, which has hosted Black-owned businesses such as Melnificent Wingz and Caribbean diasporic pop-up Rubie, as well as Palestinian home restaurant Mid East Eats. On their way out, they may circle the storefront simply named Sook to eye wines, spices, and woven goods sourced from the Levant. This is not to mention the market’s anchor restaurants: the Lebanese-influenced Maydan and Compass Rose, respectable D.C. transplants from prolific restaurateur Rose Previte, who, alongside her team, curated the market with the knockout lineup of Indigenous vendors. Maydan Market feels boldly like one whole; people rarely come for a single hyped stall. The point, in effect, is the crawl. In a year marked by ongoing, unrelenting, nationwide ICE raids targeting Black and brown immigrants, the fact that the market centers Indigenous Mexican-owned businesses, allowing their owners the space and sovereignty to reach a wider stage and audience, speaks loudly. — Nicole Fellah , dining editorial manager Marcus Jernmark. Andrea Jernmark Chef of the Year: Marcus Jernmark, Lielle and Marée Marcus Jernmark quietly landed in Los Angeles five years ago with Michelin pedigree, hosting an $800 dinner series at private homes and trying to drum up support for his own professional projects. Over time, he learned what this city was about: casual refinement, the labor of love in sourcing local ingredients, and effortless style, which he has implemented in spades at his new restaurant Lielle (and California French bistro Marée , which just opened upstairs). The results are stunning: barely cooked shrimp tangled into handmade uni pasta; fire-kissed dry-aged squab that reflects a truly joyful, energetic viewpoint. Jernmark could have shaped Lielle to be an unattainable, once-a-year dinner but instead chose a more accessible $150 prix-fixe approach — serving a menu that changes every few months to lure local diners back in to try his deceptively ambitious, inventive cooking. It’s exciting to see someone who made his career in New York, Singapore, and Stockholm embrace Los Angeles for what it is — a discerning diner’s wonderland with unparalleled food from street to tasting counter — and set a new standard. — Matthew Kang , Eater West Coast correspondent Passionfruit lime icebox pie. items.text: Dining Out in LA Your Los Angeles Restaurant Weekend Guide: November 6 Your handy guide on where to eat from the editors at Eater LA by Eater Staff Nov 6, 2026, 9:46 PM UTC Facebook Link Popcorn chicken. | Kat Thompson Dining Out in LA Your Los Angeles Restaurant Weekend Guide: November 6 Your handy guide on where to eat from the editors at Eater LA by Eater Staff Nov 6, 2026, 9:46 PM UTC Facebook Link Popcorn chicken. | Kat Thompson Facebook Link Every Friday, our editors compile a trusty list of recommendations to answer the most pressing of questions: “Where should I eat?” Here are four places to check out this weekend in Los Angeles. And if you need some ideas on where to drink, here’s our list of the hottest places to get cocktails in town. For a generous, soulful platter: Anjahles by Jazzy in West Adams Anjahles by Jazzy. Mona Holmes When the clocks fell backwards last weekend, I woke up in need of something savory and hopped in the car to find it. I remembered seeing an Instagram post by chef Jazzy Harvey , in which she bakes cornbread in a circular foil takeout container, cuts a hole in the center, then fills it with stewy oxtails, candied yams laced with rum, smoky collard greens, and a pile of creamy mac and cheese. The end of daylight saving time provided me an extra hour to chat with Harvey and watch a steady stream of folks arrive to try out her platter at her business Anjahles by Jazzy. Harvey has been operating her soulful Jamaican-LA pop-up since 2020 and has pretty much perfected her game. Pre-orders come with extras (free drink, priority pick up). Place an order through the Anjahles by Jazzy website , and pick up in West Adams on Sunday between noon and 3 p.m. 4976 West Adams Boulevard, West Adams, CA 90016. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For one last visit to a legendary spot: Everson Royce Bar in the Arts District Nachos from Everson Royce Bar. Kat Thompson If I were to build a perfect bar in my head, it might end up a lot like Everson Royce Bar in the Arts District. You enter a dim, elegant interior, but you can also continue out back to a shady patio with enough space to host a large rehearsal dinner (literally mine). Cocktails are thoughtful but unpretentious, the list of spirits is contained in a mysterious book, beer and wine are carefully curated, and there are micheladas in both red and green varieties. The food menu is short but has no skips; the biscuits and burgers are the best in town. ERB recalls a more optimistic time in the Arts District and in LA generally, characterized by casual extravagance and a sunny disposition: a Peak TV-era mindset. But that time is over, and ERB is leaving with it — the bar is closing on December 19 . That means we’ve only got a few too-short weeks to celebrate this local icon, sampling rare whiskeys and crushing smoky potato taquitos under the tree in the middle of the patio like it’s 2016 again. 1936 E. 7th Street, Los Angeles, CA 90021 . — Ben Mesirow, editor, Eater Travel For a feast of Taiwanese flavors: Sinbala in Arcadia Kat Thompson I’ve written about the magic of legendary Taiwanese restaurant Sinbala before . It’s been serving up plates of snappy Taiwanese sausage, hearty beef noodle soup, and comforting tomato egg for more than 20 years. The menu of this strip mall cafe is expansive, ranging from snackier bites like popcorn chicken and chewy fried fish cakes to more traditional Taiwanese fare like fried pork chop rice and stewed pork belly with preserved mustard greens. Whatever you end up ordering, save room for refreshing shaved ice that comes with a slew of topping options — including but not limited to bouncy rice cakes, custardy flan, and sweet canned lychee — and a glaze of burnt brown sugar syrup. 651 W. Duarte Road Suite F, Arcadia, CA 91007. — Kat Thompson, audience editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest For a mini English breakfast near LAX: Tomat in Westchester Tomat. Matthew Kang There was a never a good answer for where to eat near LAX before a mid-day flight, until Tomat opened in nearby Westchester. The handy all-day restaurant provides a peaceful morning or mid-day meal with some interesting modern British dishes that won’t weigh you down before boarding a long flight to Asia (which I did recently). The full English breakfast, usually a bit of a gutbuster, comes in a three-quarter-size portion at Tomat, featuring farmers market potatoes, house-made pudding, comforting stewed beans (not the canned variety), and half-crispy bacon. The egg is poached instead of pan-fried, and the toast is hearty sourdough. You’ll want another dish — in our case, the pastrami hash topped with a fried egg, laden with crispy chopped potatoes and plenty of fresh herbs — to feel completely full. The fermented hot sauce adds a vibrant punch and a simmering heat that will linger. Note: Breakfast is served only Wednesday to Sunday. 6261 W. 87th Street, Los Angeles, CA, 90045. — Matthew Kang, correspondent, Eater Related The 38 Best Restaurants in Los Angeles See More : Dining Out in LA Dining Out

items.text: Dining Reports Mariscos El Muelle 8 Delivers a Sensational Taste of Culiacán in Downey The new restaurant has an expanded menu, a full liquor license, and a bright, boisterous energy by Bill Esparza Nov 6, 2026, 4:40 PM UTC Facebook Link Ceviche Muelle 8 at Mariscos El Muelle 8 Bill Esparza Bill Esparza is a James Beard award-winning food journalist, author of LA Mexicano, and onscreen food television personality covering food in United States and Latin America. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Culiacán-based Mariscos El Muelle 8 has closed its East LA food truck and upgraded to a brick-and-mortar restaurant in Downey that opened on Friday, October 30. The owner of Mariscos El Muelle 8 USA , Jay Orozco, had launched the food truck in Garden Grove in 2025 after closing a previous brick-and-mortar location of Mariscos El Muelle 8 in Downey. His new 95-seat restaurant has a full liquor license and big-screen TVs for sports events. Founded in Culiacán in 2020 by Orozco’s cousin, the late Abel Martínez, Mariscos El Muelle 8 launches its new Downey restaurant with an extensive menu of barra fría (cold bar) dishes such as ceviches, aguachiles, and seafood cocktails, as well as barra caliente (hot bar) items like seafood tacos and soups. The bright cantina is ideal for sipping margaritas, micheladas, and carajillos while catching a variety of sports events (especially a Canelo fight). Mariscos El Muelle 8 delivers a unique Sinaloan seafood experience as the only Mexico-based mariscos franchise in Los Angeles. What to order Tostada lovers are in for a treat. The tostada chavita — a very Sinaloan take on the popular tuna tostada — piles cubes of sweet and sour marinated tuna on a fried wonton, with a scattering of black sesame and a crown of crispy fried onions on top. It’s a little inspiration from the sushi bar that Sinaloan chefs learned in culinary school and working at sushi bars stateside. The tostada chavita is compact and leaves plenty of room for other dishes. The shrewdest scheme to get a taste of pricey callos de hacha (pen shell clams) is in an order of Ceviche Muelle 8 , a mix of cooked shrimp, raw shrimp, cooked octopus, and those prized callos de hacha in a medium spicy salsa roja. One of the hallmarks of any barra fría is a number of variations on aguachile, a dish consisting of raw, high-quality shrimp, cured à la minute in a spicy lime juice blended with chile serrano or chile jalapeño. Ordering an aguachile negro made with the restaurant’s umami-rich salsa negra is the move; pair it with a michelada. The best seafood taco selection in town announces itself with the Taco Gaxiola , a seared strip of tuna rubbed in adobo, topped with guacamole and pico de gallo, and dressed with a chipotle-mayo. Everything zarandeado is en vogue north of the border, and camarones zarandeados are a noteworthy plate on any barra caliente. Here, large shrimp are grilled in a spicy marinade and served with undressed salad and coleslaw. The vibe The roar of crowds and booming sportscaster voices transmitted on flat-screen televisions displaying rival matches reverberate off the walls and tavern-style ceiling. The nautical-themed dining room, white with navy blue trim, features a mural depicting a day at the beach in Sinaloa. Diners are casually dressed — snapbacks are a sharp accessory for young sinaloenses — and it’s best to come with friends or family to enjoy sharable ceviches, aguachiles, and botanas (snacks). Insider tip If you want spicier, just ask when you order dishes from the barra fría. And check out the shellfish behind the bar on your right as you walk in for the day’s selection, which can include pata de mula, reina, and chocolata clams as well as Pacific oysters. Tostada chavita at Mariscos El Muelle 8.
