items.title: How to Hang a Picture Safely and Straight - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: How to Hang a Picture Safely and Straight - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content How to Hang a Picture Safely and Straight DIY & Renovate ON September 17, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content You’re standing in front of a blank wall, holding a frame with one hand and trying to decide where it should actually sit. It’s the same question my sister Renee brings me whenever she’s rearranging a room. The wall isn’t usually the difficult part. Learning how to hang a picture properly means getting three things right: placement, hardware, and the exact hook position. For a standard lightweight frame, I’d call this a 1 or 2 out of 5 DIY job that usually takes 10–30 minutes. The measuring matters more than the hammering. Get that part right, and the frame should sit securely without a trail of abandoned nail holes behind it. Picture Hanging Project Details Project Detail What To Expect Difficulty 1–2 out of 5 for a typical lightweight frame Time About 10–30 minutes Cost Low if you already own basic tools; hardware cost depends on the frame and wall Basic tools Tape measure, pencil, level, hammer or screwdriver Sometimes needed Stud finder, drill, suitable anchor Skill level Beginner for standard frames; more care is needed for heavy frames or difficult wall materials Why 57–60 Inches Is A Useful Starting Point That range approximates average adult eye level, which is why museums and galleries default to it so art reads naturally instead of forcing anyone to look up or down. In practice, most designers push that number up toward 60 inches in rooms with taller ceilings or larger art. What actually decides your number within that range is the room itself: ceiling height, nearby furniture, and how the wall reads as a whole, not any single person’s height. In a tighter room, that reading changes fast, which is exactly the judgment call behind good compact living room layouts . Treat the height range as a starting point for the room, not a fixed rule built around one viewer. Choose The Right Hanging Hardware Before measuring anything, turn the frame over. Check its weight, the hanging hardware already attached to it, and the wall you’re working with. A perfectly measured hook in the wrong type of wall fixing is still a bad installation. Picture Setup Hardware To Consider Check Before Hanging Lightweight frame Rated picture hook or suitable nail Frame weight and wall condition Sawtooth hanger Compatible nail or picture hook Sawtooth hanger is firmly attached Hanging wire Rated picture hook Wire and attachment points Two D-rings Two suitable hooks or fixings Equal height and spacing Heavy frame Rated anchor, stud fixing, or cleat Manufacturer weight rating and wall type Rental wall Rated removable hanging system when suitable Surface compatibility and product limits Don’t assume every heavier frame automatically requires a stud. Some purpose-built drywall hangers are rated for substantial loads without one. For example, 3M sells CLAW drywall hangers with specific manufacturer ratings from 15 to 65 pounds. The important part is using the exact product rating , not applying a general drywall weight rule. Plaster, masonry, tile, and drywall also behave differently. Choose hardware designed for the actual surface rather than making one type of anchor do every job. What Usually Goes Wrong First The most common mistake happens before the nail touches the wall. Someone decides where the top of the frame should sit, makes a mark, and installs the hanger there. But the hanger on the back may sit an inch, two inches, or several inches below the f

items.title: How Long to Wait Between Coats of Paint
items.text: How Long to Wait Between Coats of Paint Skip to content How Long to Wait Between Coats of Paint DIY & Renovate ON September 14, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content Paint can look ready long before it is ready for another coat. That small timing mistake is where a simple room refresh can turn into roller drag, rough patches, or extra sanding. If you are trying to figure out how long to wait between coats of paint, I would start with the recoat time on the exact product, not the clock alone. You also need to account for humidity, temperature, airflow, coat thickness, and the surface underneath. I pay closest attention to the slowest-drying areas, because they usually decide the schedule. Here, you will learn the practical timing ranges, warning signs, and checks that help you know when coat two is actually ready. How Long Should Paint Dry Before Another Coat? The manufacturer’s stated recoat time is the safest starting point. Do not judge readiness only by how quickly the surface stops feeling wet. These ranges can help with early planning: Paint or Coating Common Planning Range Main Consideration Water-based wall paint About 2–4 hours Formula and room conditions Waterborne trim or cabinet enamel About 4–16+ hours Product formulation Oil or alkyd coating Often overnight or longer Manufacturer interval Water-based primer About 1–4 hours Primer and substrate Spray or specialty coating Product-specific Minimum and maximum recoat window The differences between products can be substantial. Behr Premium Plus , for example, lists a two-hour recoat time, while Benjamin Moore ADVANCE lists 16 hours. That is why I would not schedule the second coat based only on words such as “latex,” “water-based,” or “satin.” Check the exact product first. Dry Time, Recoat Time, and Cure Time These three terms describe different stages. Dry time generally refers to when the surface no longer feels wet or tacky. Recoat time tells you when another layer can normally be applied without disturbing the first. Cure time is longer and refers to the period the coating needs to develop its intended hardness and performance. A wall can therefore feel dry while still being too early for coat two. It can also accept another coat while remaining far from fully cured. That distinction matters much more than the simple touch test. What Can Make Paint Take Longer to Recoat? A paint label gives drying information for specific application conditions. The room you are working in may not match them exactly. Temperature: Cooler conditions can slow drying. If the room is near the lower end of the product’s recommended application range, allow additional time. Humidity: Moist air can slow water loss from water-based coatings. Bathrooms, basements, kitchens, and rainy-day projects often need more patience. Airflow: Normal air circulation can help. I would not aim strong heat or a powerful fan directly at wet paint in an attempt to force the process. Coat thickness: Heavy roller passes, overlaps, textured areas, and loaded corners can stay soft longer than thin, even sections. Surface condition: Bare drywall, wood, patches, glossy paint, and sealed materials can behave differently beneath the same coating. Check the slowest area rather than the first section that feels dry. Changing the schedule is easier than repairing a damaged finish. If the Paint Feels Dry, Can You Recoat It? Not necessarily. items.title: 28 DIY Centerpieces You Can Make at Home
items.text: 28 DIY Centerpieces You Can Make at Home Skip to content 28 DIY Centerpieces You Can Make at Home DIY & Renovate ON September 14, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content My sister Renee once called before dinner because her table looked bare and every nearby store was closing. I told her to check the kitchen first. A white pitcher, three lemons, clipped greenery, and two short candles solved the problem without another purchase. That is still how I approach DIY centerpieces. Start with the table, then use the least complicated materials that suit it. Flowers, fruit, jars, branches, bowls, candles, and serving pieces can all earn a place in the middle of a table. The ideas below cover everyday meals, parties, weddings, and seasonal gatherings while keeping height, cost, and actual dining space in mind. What Makes a Homemade Table Centerpiece Work? A homemade centerpiece works when its height, width, and materials suit the table instead of taking it over. Start with one stable container, choose one main material, then add a quieter supporting element if the arrangement needs it. A pitcher with flowers, a bowl with fruit, or a tray with candles can be enough. Keep seated sightlines open and leave space for plates, glasses, and serving dishes. Repeating one flower, color, fruit, or container shape can connect several smaller pieces without making everything match. The right fix is often smaller than expected. If guests need to move the entire arrangement before dinner can begin, reduce its height or footprint. Floral and Greenery Centerpieces to Make Fresh flowers and foliage can work for an ordinary breakfast table or a larger dinner. Keep the vessel relatively quiet and allow the plant material to carry most of the shape and color. 1. Grocery Store Flowers in a Pitcher Choose one grocery-store bouquet and a sturdy pitcher with an opening narrow enough to support the stems. Trim flowers at slightly different heights and remove any leaves that would sit below the waterline. A loose arrangement usually looks better here than packing every stem tightly into place. Use fewer flowers first. You can always add another stem after checking the pitcher from a seated position. 2. Bud Vases in a Loose Row Gather five or seven small bud vases and add one or two stems to each. Repeat one flower color across the group, but vary the stem heights slightly. On a rectangular table, leave uneven spaces between the vessels rather than lining them up at identical intervals. The repetition keeps the arrangement connected while the loose spacing prevents it from feeling overly formal. 3. Garden Branches in a Tall Vase One or two branching stems can fill considerable visual space without requiring a large bouquet. Use a heavy vase that will not tip, then rotate each branch until its more open side faces the room. Keep this arrangement on a large dining table, console, or buffet where the height will not interfere with conversation. If branches cross directly through a seated guest’s sightline, move them rather than adding more material around the base. 4. Low Flower Bowl A shallow bowl is one of the easiest ways to make flowers work on a round dining table. Cut the stems short enough to sit near the rim. Begin with one main flower in the center, then work outward with smaller flowers or restrained greenery. The low shape gives the centerpiece presence without forcing guests to look around it during dinner. 5. items.title: Aurora Borealis (Northern Lights) – Southern Ontario
items.text: You are here: Home / Landscape / Aurora Borealis (Northern Lights) – Southern Ontario Due to prior commitment, I missed the spectacular Northern Lights display on Friday night when it had the intensity of G8. Last night, the intensity was forecasted as G5 and actually weakened to G3. Anyway, I ventured out trying my luck with no expectations . I arrived the site at midnight and stay till 2:30am. I was not disappointed as I was able to capture a few images when it was active very briefly for about 10 minutes at 12:38am. items.title: https://clbarchitects.com/process/
items.text: Process | CLB Architects Process Across three decades of practice, we have honed a design language that brings people in intimate dialogue with place. Our collaborative, inquisitive culture informs our design approach from start to finish. We believe the creative process is a journey, and one that can reveal something greater than initially imagined. We relish this process of discovery. Architecture + Interiors No matter the scale, we design as a whole—architecture and interiors united in a creative vision that begins and ends together. Land + Vision Every project begins with place. We shape spaces that respond to their setting, whether in rugged landscapes, urban centers, or cultural contexts, so that each design grows authentically from its site. Concept + Collaboration Our design concepts grow out of conversation and discovery, becoming a clear framework that directs the full arc of a project’s journey. Making Predictability is the foundation of a project’s success. By documenting with rigor and foresight, we ensure that builders can execute each element with precision, efficiency, and integrity. Realization Throughout the process, we remain dedicated partners, guiding projects through construction to ensure that what is built reflects the vision we began together. Interested in working with us? Let’s start a conversation. Our team works across scales and settings to shape architecture and interiors that endure. Contact Us

items.title: https://clbarchitects.com/projects/shinemaker/
items.text: ShineMaker | CLB Architects Watch Film ShineMaker Wilson, Wyoming Service Architecture Type Residential Location Wilson, Wyoming Photography Matthew Millman Douglas Friedman Aaron Kraft Video: Sheets Studios A series of undulating structures set against an aspen grove near Wilson, Wyoming, this mountain home serves as a creative retreat for a California-based couple. The 35-acre property is set at the base of the Tetons and encompasses several ecosystems, with old-growth forest merging into stands of young pine and aspen trees before transitioning into rolling meadows. Composed of three buildings (main house, guest house, and writer’s studio), the home is arranged as a set of simple box-like volumes, each designed in response to its specific location. The 6,000-square-foot main house is conceived as a geologic remnant in the landscape, located on the edge between field and forest. The 1,577-square-foot guest house and 580-square-foot writer’s studio are nestled more intimately within the wooded environment. A fourth, spiritually focused structure was recently completed and sited further to the south. Throughout all buildings, the architecture is open, with sweeping views to mountain vistas of the Grand Tetons, natural fauna, forests, and meadows. Rectilinear in plan, the main house appears to grab surrounding trees as anchors, sinking in the center, and pulling upward toward the sky at the corners. Working in concert with the landscape, this dynamic quality is carried through the building’s charred shou sugi ban exterior, tugged and carved to create overhangs and openings. The wood exterior wraps into the interior as light Atlantic cedar, which then dissolves into subtle plaster and floor-to-ceiling glass. Creative Retreat The homeowners, authors who also own and manage an independent record label out of Mill Valley, California, were looking for a nature-oriented outpost in Wyoming in which to pursue their writing practice. Their bohemian lifestyle and love of music, literature, and the great outdoors inspired the interior design, which emphasizes layers, texture, and comfort. The earth-toned palette is punctuated by collectible pieces, vintage finds, and contemporary art. Framing Nature The entrance to the home is located where the structure reaches out over a lowland creek, the relationship revealed by a moment of transparency in the floor. Inside, each window frames a view of the prairie and Teton range beyond. An east-facing fireplace provides a counterpoint to the views, and an intimate courtyard allows southern light to penetrate the center of the home. Project Leads Contact Us Andy Ankeny AIA Partner Eric Logan FAIA Partner Sam Ankeny AIA Principal Project Collaborators Interior Design HSH Interiors

items.title: https://clbarchitects.com/projects/riverbend/
items.text: Riverbend | CLB Architects Watch Film Riverbend Jackson, Wyoming Service Architecture Interiors + Objects Type Residential Location Jackson, Wyoming Photography Matthew Millman Tom Harris Video: Sheets Studios This private residence is located on an 18-acre wooded property on the east bank of the Snake River adjacent to Grand Teton National Park. A careful study of the river resulted in a design that engages with its riverine and mountain setting, marking its difference and deference to the landscape. Located on a wooded property with dramatic mountain views, this house sits adjacent to the Snake River, which forms the north and west perimeter of the site. A careful consideration of the relationship between the building envelope, river, and mountain views led to the decision to elevate the main floor of the house six feet above the natural ground plane. The main and guest houses surround a south-facing deck and a bosquet of aspen trees. Resting on bases of board-formed concrete, the volumes are defined by large overhangs sheltering deep-set glazing, and associated decks that unify the architecture. On the whole, the design strikes a balance between exposure and enclosure, contrasting broad glass expanses and open volumes with textures and materials that offer a sense of grounded comfort. Engaging with Nature On the river side, a protected deck runs the length of the house, rising to the second story on the east. This multipurpose outdoor space serves as an extension of the living room, dining, and kitchen, and provides access to the river via a series of platforms. Patina Cedar interior and exterior walls are enclosed in an exterior shell of weathering steel. Over time, the steel will develop a patina and the home will exchange its black shell for a rusty one, helping it further integrate into its site, much like a rusty pickup truck forgotten in the landscape. Project Leads Contact Us Kevin Burke AIA, LEED AP Partner Eric Logan FAIA Partner Bryan James AIA, LEED AP Principal Libby Erker Senior Designer

items.title: https://clbarchitects.com/projects/caju/
items.text: Caju | CLB Architects Watch Film Caju Teton Village, Wyoming Service Architecture Interiors + Objects Type Residential Location Teton Village, Wyoming Photography Matthew Millman Video: Sheets Studios Caju is a home where simplicity and honesty of materials are derived from the belief that there is beauty in functionality. The name “Caju” is borrowed from a Brazilian fruit with an orange shell, similar to the home’s weathered steel exterior. Caju began when a young family based in Miami sought a serene retreat at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort. With roots in Brazil and a deep appreciation for the outdoors, they envisioned an intimate and welcoming house where their family and occasional guests could connect and unwind. Their brief emphasized living simply—a home designed for the essentials rather than excess—grounded in practicality and natural materiality. Located on one of the last undeveloped parcels in Teton Village, the site is defined by dense timber, rugged topography, and striking views of the Snake River Valley and surrounding peaks. The heavily wooded and boulder-strewn lot required a sensitive design approach, minimizing tree removal and site disturbance. The resulting structure is both embedded in and hovering above the landscape, with a compact footprint and an elevated bedroom wing supported by slender columns that touch the hillside lightly. This approach preserves the integrity of the terrain while offering heightened perspectives of the area’s natural splendor. Outdoor spaces, including a rear metal grate deck that encircles a pair of aspen trees and a front deck extending from the kitchen offering prospecting valley views, further enhance the home’s integration with its environment. Weathering Steel Materiality is at the core of the project’s identity, with a palette restricted to steel, wood, and concrete. These durable and humble materials were chosen for their ability to age gracefully and for their inherent beauty. The living finish of the weathered Corten steel exterior provides a dynamic backdrop for the natural surroundings. Natural Light The two-story layout strategically positions the main living areas on the upper floor to maximize views, while the lower level houses practical spaces such as a garage, mudroom, and gym. The upper level features an open-plan living, dining, and kitchen area along with four bedrooms. A floating staircase—a perforated stainless steel structure—serves as both a functional and sculptural element, visually connecting the two levels and allowing light to filter through. Project Leads Contact Us Eric Logan FAIA Partner Andy Ankeny AIA Partner Jeffrey Johnston Associate Maria James LEED AP Associate

The breadth of the collection consists of 137 sculptures, 87 bases, 41 drawings, 2 paintings and over a thousand glass-plate negatives & original prints. The continuation of the artwork’s soul, the artist’s mind, all within these walls, live on. “For Brancusi, the space created as the surrounding for sculpture is as important as the work itself, and it was in his studio that he was best able to do this. The studio became an entity into which he gradually incorporated the ‘doubles’ of his original works, whereby he was more perfectly able to preserve their memory.” I arrived to the Atelier as the staff dusted off their chairs and repositioned a fresh stack of pamphlets, braced to wade through crowds of people curiously exploring the studio through their iPhones. I knew Paris to be a location of galleries and museums with no shortage of crowds, however I didn’t find myself any more comfortable with it despite the grandiose caliber of each institution. I didn’t even visit the Louvre for this reason. Admittedly, I fantasized about a lonesome experience like the cake I knew I couldn’t bake but wanted anyway. This day was different. To any tourist’s amazement, and for this one time, my fears of anxiously pushing my way to the front were dismissed. I had the glassed-off, windex-polished corridor to myself for several minutes. Even to share that detail doesn’t seem all that impressive, but the several minutes I shared half-past two in the heat of the afternoon were the most calming minutes of my entire time spent in Paris. “They assume their place quite naturally, under the peak of the roof meeting the skylight, squeezed against one another like lofty trees in a tropical forest, facing the entrance. ‘This studio is my garden: here I am alone and happy!’ Said Brancusi.” At the end of his life, Brancusi became enveloped by the spatial relationships of the sculptures within his studio. In fact, if a piece had been sold, Brancusi would replace the void with a plaster copy. The dialog between works and the studio walls became fundamental enough for him to stop creating artworks and to focus on the presentation as a whole. Why I take to Brancusi is fairly simple: We consider the essence apex. The calm curves and hues of ecru are inviting, but deeply spiritual in the context of the space. Born in Detroit and now lives in Los Angeles. She is a capricorn and makes conspicuous playlists . Social ︎︎︎ Email ︎︎︎ Instagram Substack Newsletter ︎︎︎ Sign up here Interviews ︎︎︎ A Time of Gifts - How to Search for Utopia at Sea Ranch ︎︎︎ Flying B Magazine ︎︎︎ VSCO ︎︎︎ MOUTHWASH ︎︎︎ VoyageLA ︎︎︎ Shoutout LA ︎︎︎ Rikkes Space ︎︎︎ Present Joys by Present Studio Press, Accolades ︎︎︎ Architectural Digest Top 100 Photographers ︎︎︎ The Brand Identity ︎︎︎ Dwell ︎︎︎Longlisted - Best Project Photography 2024 Créateurs Design Awards Writing ︎︎︎ A Map of the World ︎︎︎ Learning How to See in San Miguel de Allende ︎︎︎Untogetherness ︎︎︎Atelier Brancusi ︎︎︎Ten Thousand Things by Edmund de Waal Selected Clients include Architectural Digest, Domino Magazine, Dwell, Cultured Mag, Monocle, The Panafold, Kinfolk, Miller Knoll, Soho House, Vogue, VSCO and LVMH, has photographed Instagram and Nike Headquarters, and frequently works with top interior design firms, furniture makers and galleries; The Future Perfect, Commune, Carpenters Workshop Gallery, Emeco, Kalon Studios, Klein Agency, Fyrn and Francis Gallery. © Elizabeth Carababas 2026 ︎︎︎ Back Modular Mind / Ten Thousand Things by Edmund de Waal "It is about what it means to belong in one place at one time" - Edmund de Waal Poetry of Paul Celan and musical compositions by John Cage were both pioneering pools of inspiration for de Waal's latest ceramic work. Cage's personal accords with Taoism and Chinese modular patterns of thought serves as a basis for de Waal. Endless repetition, indefinite multitudes; the hand-formed vessels serve gracefully to therapeutic processes and zen-like mastery of obsessive repetitive work. We think of Donald Judd because of sequence of form or Serra for uses of dense material to elude to a weightlessness. Feng Shui is not stagnant. Cream and white-mint. Fingerprint of gold on its lip and coy curves welcoming to palm of the hand. Each vessel is dainty to the extent they ought to be tangible. Great art, great prints, wonderful paintings and sculptures of the smaller scale feel accessible, tactile, on a level our minds and body can intake with ease. Even in large glazed frames of shelves it lacks a deprecation to our egos: "larger than us". We can peer in with a closeness you could count the grains of metallic. But the warmth of openness is barricaded by glass and you can not participate actively. With the vessels rearranged in close quarters of metal and steel cages, I feel less warm with the pieces than I do with those in architectural spaces open to the possibility of my touch. Staggered in balanced alphabet of Morris Code they exist like a mind map. A pattern of DNA or a hieroglyph of de Waal's undercurrent of the subconscious. The art was born into a vacuum and thus adopts a disposition from its confinement. What is the relationship of the restricted vessels with their real estate? Why do I feel alone? We work with being, but non-being is what we use. -Tao te Ching by Lao Tzu The entirety of the exhibition that oscillates between a confinement of materials, minimalism and staggering of placement, economy of materials and palettes--even with their dichotomizations--is very much a statement, perhaps indirectly, on a western vs eastern headspace. After all, the precious utilization of a cup is its emptiness. And emptiness is openness for solitude. Confine it behind a barrier in a controlled environment and it reiterates the philosophy that architecture is inherently and arguably the most influential medium to our lives. Edmund de Waal's Ten Thousand Things at Gagosian Gallery, Beverly Hills 2016

items.title: AvroKO — Reading Club & Seneca
items.text: San Diego , CA USA Reading Club & Seneca Members Club & Restaurant , Est. San Diego , CA USA Members Club & Restaurant , Est. About A rooftop dining room and members club with designs inspired by nautical traditions, seaside locales, maritime detailing, and the spirit of exploration. They celebrate not just the bounty of discovery, but the journey itself. Nautical inspirations serve as the through line for The Reading Club and Seneca Trattoria. The Reading Club's identity is influenced by the many historic ships that passed through the San Diego Harbor. Seneca Trattoria took inspiration from the nautical mess halls and communal dining in tight quarters, which fostered a sense of community among the ship's passengers during the long voyage. Restaurant & Bar Design Awards Best Standalone Restaurant LOCATION San Diego , CA USA Size 3,800 ft² / 353 m² CaTEGORY Food & Beverage Client Consortium Holdings Keys On The Fringe Meticulous details with a maritime spirit. Inlaid copper strips use flag semaphore to spell out secret messages when tables are arranged a certain way. Textured holophane glass on light fixtures refracts light similar to lighthouses and ship deck lighting. Tassels on furniture capture the ever-present sway and motion while sailing. A feature, streamline 1940’s banquette brings in a WWII pin-up vibe found on ships of that era. Open Gallery Fringe, tassels, bold patterns and colors, and signature graphics pull the daring design together. Nautical Nuance Both The Reading Club and Seneca Trattoria rely on materials typically found on different types of ocean liners to create spaces rich in maritime culture. The Reading Club draws on the disappearing craft of shipbuilding that historically focused on the use of wood, while the aim with Seneca Trattoria was to blend high-craft detailing with utilitarian nautical functionality giving it a more modern look and feel. High-gloss wood floors, metal-paneled walls with exposed rivets, and copper ceilings are just a few of the materials on display. No items found. items.title: AvroKO — Centara Reserve
items.text: Koh Samui , Thailand Centara Reserve Luxury Resort , Est. Koh Samui , Thailand Luxury Resort , Est. About Centara Reserve is a contemporary beach resort located on the island of Samui in the Gulf of Thailand. The overarching design concept pulls inspiration from both the existing colonial envelope as well as from the traditional craft of decorative Thai wood carving. The wood carving is brought into a contemporary context with simplified silhouettes and geometric forms. An unexpected layer that also pervades throughout is a sense of defying gravity, with sculptural elements that appear to be simultaneously light and heavy. Lifestyle Asia "Subtle yet familiar, refreshing and exciting, and coincidentally or not, really Instagrammable." LOCATION Koh Samui , Thailand Size 24,520 ft² / 2.278 m² CaTEGORY Hotels & Residential Client Centara Hotels & Resorts Keys 184 Open Gallery Elevated Arrival At the arrival, an elevated runway draws guests into the dramatic and light-filled lobby. Two columns at the end of the runway perfectly frame a dramatic, tiered chandelier that hovers in the middle of the lobby space. The chandelier has sculpted wood arms, reminiscent of Thai vernacular details, but is juxtaposed with cleaner metalwork joinery and a modern overall form. No items found. Centara Reserve Koh Samui , Thailand OF OF No items found. No items found. The Gin Bar To the right of the lobby lies the Gin Bar. Enclosed in a rotunda, its architecture is reminiscent of a grand sunroom one might find in a colonial estate. The interior, however, is very much a departure from anything traditional, with a bold blue, gray and white terrazzo floor, and a sculptural bar. The design concept merges detailing from historical apothecaries with geometric forms extracted from traditional Thai indigo textiles. No items found. No items found. "Sleek design and architecture." items.title: AvroKO — Oiji Mi
items.text: New York , NY USA Oiji Mi Restaurant & Bar , Est. New York , NY USA Restaurant & Bar , Est. About Oiji Mi is a Michelin-starred, modern Korean restaurant and bar by acclaimed chef Brian Kim. The space is simultaneously nostalgic and modern, merging two contrasting themes: the traditional Korean hanok (home) and the early 20th century social clubs of NYC’s Flatiron District, in which this venue resides. We wanted guests to feel like they were straddling two places in a liminal state - not quite Korea and not quite New York. We aimed to design a transporting space that heightened senses for guests to be keenly attuned to the precision of the tasting menu. Chef-owner Brian Kim digs into his Korean roots to craft food that is not only exquisite, but also visually breathtaking. Our space aimed to complement the tones, colors and textures captured in his creations. Artwork in the space is all derived from various Korean textile techniques. Handcrafted Korean traditional quilting called Jo-Gak-Bo, appears backlit from the ceiling. A delicate translucent screen with subtle colored thread divides the bar from the restaurant. Thrillist A "gorgeous space." LOCATION New York , NY USA Size 5,100 ft² / 474 m² CaTEGORY Food & Beverage Client Oiji Hospitality Group Keys Harmony Between Food and Space Traditional yet elevated Chef-owner Brian Kim delivers fine dining with fun and imagination, serving up his modern renditions of Korean classics. The space is harmonious and warm. The color palette, with gentle pinks and greens, has a serenity that allows the sensational food to take center stage on the table. Open Gallery There is a strong, symbiotic relationship between the environment and the food. Korean Hanok The layout of the traditional Korean home, or hanok, drove the architecture of the space. The main dining room is framed by doubled-up wood beams characteristic of Korean buildings. The space mimics a traditional exterior courtyard in plan and through finishes like rustic timber and pebbled stone flooring. Smaller spaces radiate from the courtyard center dining - seating nooks, the wine rooms, and the open kitchen. No items found. Oiji Mi New York , NY USA OF OF No items found. No items found. Cool Tones, Warm Finishes We layered in the glamour found in the 20th century Flatiron social clubs through plush seating, ornamental brass, and filigree details in the lighting. We complemented that with design vernacular found in traditional Korean architecture, and then wrapped the whole thing in a palette of warm plum, powder blue and cool green - inspired by traditional Korean color palettes. No items found. No items found. "Fun and beautiful indeed. Both attributes are apparent in every aspect of Oiji Mi’s hospitality experience, putting it into a category all its own. Traditional Korean accessories called norigae inspired custom pendants that are illuminated below beautiful knot rope details in the main dining space. Four delicate lights sit on the back bar mimicking the design and craft of traditional Korean hair pins. items.title: AvroKO — Single Thread
items.text: Healdsburg , CA USA Single Thread Farm, Restaurant & Inn , Est. Healdsburg , CA USA Farm, Restaurant & Inn , Est. About Single Thread is a three Michelin Star restaurant, farm and inn in Healdsburg, CA. The AvroKO team found its inspiration for the design in husband and wife team and owners, Kyle and Katina Connaughton. In understanding that a restaurant is not only a place to eat, but also a functioning studio for its craftsmen, AvroKO created a dining experience that is akin to spending an evening with Kyle and Katina in their personal workshop, where diners are given the opportunity to both observe the artistic process and enjoy its end product. Elements of the ‘studio’ are found throughout the dining room: silverware is stored in one of seven hand-numbered drawers that label which course it is used for; ceramic vessels found in various storage units appear to be decorative until the Chef fetches them for a specific course during the night; a glass terrarium serves as both a beautiful visual and a workspace for Katina to build nightly flower displays. Odes to the couple’s love for farming, gardening, and molecular gastronomy can also be found throughout the space. James Beard Design Awards Best Restaurant Design LOCATION Healdsburg , CA USA Size 9,200 ft² / 855 m² CaTEGORY Food & Beverage Client Up Ventures LLC Keys Dream Team A three Michelin Star experience in the heart of wine country Born from an obsessive passion for nuance, craft and innovation, this modern Californian Ryokan is filled with lovingly personal touches and an unwavering commitment to exceptional guest experience. Japan meets Northern California in this exacting culinary destination. Open Gallery High-touch details abound at Single Thread Fibonacci and the Farm Given Katina’s abilities to understand the micro-nuances of farming and gardening, and Kyle’s experiences with molecular gastronomy, AvroKO found inspiration in the science and mathematics of nature. Fibonacci sequences and golden sections that come from natural growth patterns and natural proportions played heavily into the design, driving material transitions, tile proportions, patterns, and layouts. Floating ceiling panels have grids that highlight golden section relationships, as do the kitchen tile patterns, the leather wrapped columns, the dining room screens, and the oversized custom wood entry door. Sliding brass and fabric doors that divide the kitchen and dining room have an abstracted Fibonacci proportion that is only revealed in full once the doors are closed towards meal’s end. No items found. Single Thread Healdsburg , CA USA OF The DNA is in the Details Woven patterns within the dining room screens, constructed of loom components and parts, reference DNA sequencing of common kitchen herbs like basil and shallots, and showcase Kyle’s understanding of molecular structure and properties of food. These ephemeral and delicate room dividers add a reverent hush to the space. OF Organizing Principles Architecturally, AvroKO looked to the Villa Mairea, where Alvar Aalto showcases not just a final project, but rather a series of studies on form, material, and detail that compose the final product. As a device to solve for inconvenient structural column locations left over from the building’s previous tenant, AvroKO referenced Aalto’s column types in Villa Mairea to hide the building's existing structure and also define a central dining area. Each column type has a specific leather-wrapped banding pattern, hand-stitched to the column in situ that nods to many of the other Scandinavian craftsmen working during Aalto’s era. No items found. No items found. "All of these threads are woven together seamlessly in a sophisticated AvroKO-designed space that's rich in meaning and exceptional in details." items.title: AvroKO — Quality Bistro
items.text: New York , NY Quality Bistro Restaurant & Bar , Est. New York , NY Restaurant & Bar , Est. About Following in the footsteps of Quality Meats and Quality Italian, the design for Quality Bistro explores dedicated, regional influences mixed with an imaginative, storied personae. Whereas Quality Meats was inspired by a turn of the 20th-century New York butcher shop and tenement apartment, and Quality Italian a 1930’s apothecary and Tuscan villa, Quality Bistro explores the French countryside as its point of departure, capturing the spirit of a fictionalized Belle Époque era hotel rediscovered in the 1970’s, overrun by the outside gardens and gilded with mirrored walls and Opaline chandeliers throughout. While Quality Meats celebrates the cow and Quality Italian the boar, Quality Bistro trumpets all manner of fowl, with birds in framed scenes or painted throughout directly on the wood columns, tiled walls, and caned panels. Elite Traveler The World's Best New Restaurants LOCATION New York , NY Size 5,000 ft² / 465 m² CaTEGORY Food & Beverage Client Quality Branded Keys Open Gallery La Salle à Manger The different dining rooms are arranged as a series of layers that flow into each other as defined volumes, but not full enclosures, all with permeable partitions and boundaries. The main dining room has a two tone basketweave wood flooring, a series of custom chandeliers marching down the soaring 18’ ceiling, and a feature custom wine cabinet wall. A 16’ tall high gloss arched back bar with antique mirror and brass glowing shelves greets guests as they enter the venue. Custom leather, canine and glossy powder coated bar stools stand along the rich walnut sculptural bar die and counter top featuring custom bar lamps. A majestic 9’ diameter, custom chandelier with opaline glass emitting a warm glow hangs high above, filling the acoustical linen and painted wood trim floating ceiling. No items found. Quality Bistro New York , NY OF OF No items found. No items found. French Bistro Reinterpreted The burnt orange leather pullman booths along the windows dressed with cafe curtains feature integrated custom light fixtures with brass overhead coat racks inspired by classic french bistros but reinterpreted in fresh finishes and forms. Hand-painted murals of wild birds sit throughout the space, breaking their wood framed boundaries and consume the wall surfaces. Custom zinc tables with orange painted accents balance the rich textures of the plantings and the cozy furnishings. No items found. No items found. "A majestic multi-level spin on the French brasserie." Eater NY Open Gallery Le Conservatoire As you enter the first dining room, The Conservatory, a 60 year old rubber tree surrounded with leather and velvet plush Hollywood banquettes pull the guests into a dreamlike overgrown garden. A variety of plants hang off of the overhead trellises, bulkheads, and combined with the potted plants scattered around the seating, create a magical indoor oasis. The mirror wall renders a modern take on Belle Epoque’s ornate wall dressings with intricate, three dimensional moldings surrounding mirrors. Composed of different types of antiqued mirror pieces butt jointed together, this wall of mirror gracefully reflects the lush greenery within the room, amplifying the enveloping garden feel. items.text: The Empty Corner Happening DOES ORIGINAL STILL EXIST? Watch a recording of the event > November 14th 2024 Share A panel of creative experts debating the value of originality today. ​ ​ Featuring: Clemence Pirajean, Co-Founder, Pirajean Lees Kate Shepherd, Executive Producer Ben Weaver, Editor-in-Chief, The London List Moderated by Elizabeth Choppin, Editor-in-Chief of Design Anthology UK design antho/ogy UK x PIRAJEAN LEES Please subscribe to watch the video 'Happenings' at Pirajean Lees began this week at the studio on Burnsall Street, Chelsea. What were the burning questions amongst this industry-leading, eclectic creative audience? Elizabeth Choppin, Editor-in-Chief of Design Anthology UK, moderated the panel and the open discussion about the value of originality today. Pirajean Lees HAPPENING | DOES ORIGINAL STILL EXIST? press to zoom Pirajean Lees HAPPENING | DOES ORIGINAL STILL EXIST? press to zoom Pirajean Lees HAPPENING | DOES ORIGINAL STILL EXIST? press to zoom Pirajean Lees HAPPENING | DOES ORIGINAL STILL EXIST? press to zoom 1/11 The event was a passionate dialogue from the perspectives of interior design, art history, film, music and creativity at large. ​ Audience participation added to the rich tapestry of ideas presented at the evening which also provided a platform for networking in a celebration of all areas of creative production. Stories from the panel and the audience were not only deeply insightful, the topic brought to light personal anecdotes. We are deeply appreciative of our panel and guests for being so open and generous with their knowledge and network. Ben Weaver's incredibly eloquent delivery of the evolution of creativity and trends over the centuries and Kate Shepherd's insights from the entertainment industry and AI were beautifully juxtaposed with Clemence Pirajean's analogue approach to narrative Interior Architecture. This is the first in a series of 'Happenings' at Pirajean Lees. We are planning further creative events to bring together talent and encourage open discussion, insight and collaboration. ​ The next 'Happening' will be in February. items.title: Barefoot Luxury in the Balearics | PIRAJEAN LEES
items.text: The Empty Corner New Beginnings in the Balearics RENOVATING A FAMILY HOLIDAY HOME IN THE BALEARICS November 5th 2024 Share Founders Clemence Pirajean and James Lees are on-site exploring the seascape and landscape surrounds of a traditional house in the Balearics. Unusually, we are designing whilst demolishing to expedite the reinvention of our family holiday home in time for handover in spring 2025, before the summer season begins. ​​​ This traditional Mediterranean property is rich with soul. We will be reconfiguring, restoring and reinvigorating the space and its surroundings to create a unique high-end family holiday home. We will be preserving the charming and quirky features that we have discovered. Modernising does not mean knocking to the ground and starting again. We are sensitive to celebrating history and want to ensure that this new chapter in the building's life integrates all of the elements that instil it with so much personality. We are designing a peaceful sanctuary, surrounded by nature. James is sketching on-site in the warmth of the autumnal Mediterrannean sun. Clemence is reconfiguring on location. We sit on every seat in the house to understand how it feels and how it will be used by our family and guests. ​ ​ It is rare that we have the opportunity to document and publish the design and build of a residential project as they are usually under strict confidentiality. Subscribe to messages from The Empty Corner to follow our process and progress in the Balearics. Designing a family home is a very personal journey. items.title: Inside the Studio of Narrative Designers | PIRAJEAN LEES
items.text: The Empty Corner Inside the Studio INSIDE THE STUDIO OF NARRATIVE DESIGNERS PIRAJEAN LEES November 10th 2024 Share Our headquarters are on Burnsall Street, within a converted workshop just a few steps from London’s Kings Road—an iconic postcode that represents decades of independent creativity, experimentalism and eccentricity. The lofty creative space houses our team of free-thinking designers, charged with the studio’s ethos of creating richly imaginative interiors that stand the test of time. In the studio you’ll find many of our bespoke objects, unusual fabrics, stained glass, artisanal wooden beads and furniture ‘Edition’ pieces. These are iconic pieces handcrafted by our artisans. This is our day-to-day workplace, functionally designed to fill our team and our guests with elegant calm and curiosity, offering a breath of fresh air from predictable design. Our ethos is meaningful and bespoke design with purpose. Furniture is made-to-measure—honouring heritage, craft and above all, originality, people and place. We create memorable experiences and talking points. ​ By day the studio thrives with clients, friends and colleagues who are welcomed with warm pastries, charcoal-filtered water and design savoir-faire. By night it is repurposed as a hub for design industry happenings . Vinyl is played, the wine is poured and industry friends and thought leaders congregate to collaborate, discuss and invigorate the design industry. The studio is known for its warmth and open-minded collaboration. But most significantly for our narrative design which sets intelligent style and (oftentimes wild) creativity free. Our oval boardroom table is crafted from an ancient oak tree that fell in a storm, the first in a limited edition soon to be released. The grain of the wood has been left intact, unpolished, and is a design feature that allows the natural character of the wood to tell its own beautiful story. "We fell in love with this workshop at first sight. Not because of how it looked as it was stuck in the 1990s, but for its soul. There’s a feeling when you walk through a space and it feels right. Here, we could feel its creative ancestry as a workshop and good energy. When we first visited, everything was aesthetically wrong; the spatial arrangement was wrong, there were tiny doors everywhere, but the volume was great and we could see what it could become. ​ ​A space can look at its very worst but we can see it at its future best, instantly. We could see through the dingy office walls that we were presented with. We could visualise walls moving and light pouring in. As Interior Architects, this is what we love most—we can transform buildings into completely new spaces. ​The studio's loftiness now provides incredible daylight with a ceiling height that is rarely found in prime London. We have restored the old workshop and harnessed its character, transforming it to the perfect home for our design and Architecture creatives and to receive our clients and guests." ​ ​ ​ Clemence Pirajean & James Lees When we receive a compelling brief or RFP, we invite our potential clients to our studio for a workshop. This is when we have a chemistry and creative meeting to explain our unconventional and highly effective creative process. Our unique way of working creates a narrative for the project that results in the creation of truly original spaces, timeless designs of distinction that will be appreciated for many years to come.
